verses.127:1: A Song of Ascents. Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in His ways.
verses.127:2: You shall eat the fruits of your labors; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you.
verses.127:3: Your wife shall be like a flourishing vine along the sides of your house; your sons like newly planted olive shoots around your table.
verses.127:4: Behold, so shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed.
verses.127:5: May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life,
verses.127:6: and may you see the sons of your sons. Peace upon Israel.
verses.128:1: A Song of Ascents. "Many times they have warred against me from my youth," let Israel now say—
verses.128:2: "Many times they have warred against me from my youth, yet indeed they could not prevail against me."
verses.128:3: Upon my back the sinners hammered; they prolonged their iniquity.
verses.128:4: The righteous Lord has severed the neck of sinners.
verses.128:5: Let them be put to shame and turned backward, all who hate Zion.
verses.128:6: Let them become like grass of the housetops, which withers before it is plucked up,
verses.128:7: with which the harvester does not fill his hand, nor he who gathers the sheaves his bosom;
verses.128:8: and those who pass by do not say, "The blessing of the Lord be upon us; we will bless you in the name of the Lord."
verses.129:1: A Song of Ascents. From the depths I have cried out to You, O Lord;
verses.129:2: Lord, listen to my voice; let Your ears give heed to the voice of my supplication.
verses.129:3: If You should observe iniquities, O Lord—O Lord, who shall endure?
verses.129:4: For with You there is propitiation. For the sake of Your name,
verses.129:5: I have waited, O Lord; my soul has waited for His law.
verses.129:6: My soul has hoped in the Lord from the morning watch until night;
verses.129:7: for with the Lord is mercy, and abundant redemption is with Him,
verses.129:8: and He Himself shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
verses.130:1: A Song of Ascents. O Lord, my heart has not been lifted up, nor have my eyes been raised on high; nor have I walked in great matters, nor in wondrous things beyond me,
verses.130:2: but rather I was humble-minded. And I lifted up my soul, like a weaned child toward its mother, until You recompense my soul.
verses.130:3: Let Israel hope in the Lord from now and forevermore.
verses.131:1: A Song of Ascents. Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness,
verses.131:2: how he swore to the Lord, and vowed to the God of Jacob:
verses.131:3: "Surely I will not enter the dwelling of my house, nor ascend upon the couch of my bed;
verses.131:4: I will not give sleep to my eyes, nor slumber to my eyelids, nor rest to my temples,
verses.131:5: until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob."
verses.131:6: Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the thickets of the forest.
verses.131:7: I will enter into His dwellings; we will worship at the place where His feet stood.
verses.131:8: Arise, O Lord, into Your rest, You and the ark of Your holiness.
verses.131:9: Your priests have clothed themselves with righteousness, and Your holy ones shall rejoice.
verses.131:10: For the sake of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed.
verses.131:11: The Lord swore truth to David, and He will by no means annul it: "From the fruit of your body I will set one upon your throne.
verses.131:12: If your sons keep My covenant and these testimonies of Mine which I will teach them, their sons also shall sit upon your throne forever."
verses.131:13: For the Lord has selected Zion; He has chosen her as a habitation for Himself:
verses.131:14: "This is My resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.
verses.131:15: I will surely bless her widow; her poor I will satisfy with bread.
verses.131:16: I will clothe her priests with salvation, and her holy ones shall rejoice with exultation.
verses.131:17: There I will cause a horn to spring forth for David; I have prepared a lamp for your anointed.
verses.131:18: I will clothe his enemies with shame, but upon him My holiness shall blossom."
verses.132:1: A Song of Ascents. Behold now, what is good or what is pleasant, except for brethren to dwell together as one?
verses.132:2: It is like fragrant oil upon the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, running down upon the border of his garment;
verses.132:3: like the dew of Hermon, descending upon the mountains of Zion; for there the Lord commanded the blessing and life forevermore.
verses.133:1: A Song of Ascents. Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord, who stand in the courts of the house of our God.
verses.133:2: In the nights, lift up your hands toward the sanctuary, and bless the Lord.
verses.133:3: The Lord shall bless you from Zion, He who made heaven and earth.
verses.134:1: Hallelujah. Praise the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you servants,
verses.134:2: who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.
verses.134:3: Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing psalms to His name, for it is lovely;
verses.134:4: for the Lord has chosen Jacob for Himself, Israel for His own treasured possession.
verses.134:5: For I have come to know that the Lord is great, and that our Lord is above all the gods.
verses.134:6: All that the Lord willed, He has done, in heaven and on earth, in the seas and in the deeps;
verses.134:7: bringing up clouds from the farthest end of the earth, He has made lightnings for the rain; He brings forth winds from His treasuries.
verses.134:8: He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to beast;
verses.134:9: He sent forth signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh and upon all his servants.
verses.134:10: He struck many nations and slew mighty kings—
verses.134:11: Sihon king of the Amorites, and Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan—
verses.134:12: and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel His servant.
verses.134:13: O Lord, Your name endures forever; O Lord, Your memorial is from generation to generation.
verses.134:14: The Lord has compassion on His people, and concerning His servants He will be comforted.
verses.134:15: The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the works of the hands of men.
verses.134:16: They have a mouth, yet do not speak; they have eyes, yet will not see;
verses.134:17: they have ears, yet will not give ear; for neither is there any breath in their mouth.
verses.134:18: May all who make them become like them, and all who put their trust in them.
verses.134:19: O house of Israel, bless the Lord; O house of Aaron, bless the Lord;
verses.134:20: O house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.
verses.134:21: Blessed is the Lord from Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem.
verses.135:1: Hallelujah. Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy abides forever.
verses.135:2: Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy abides forever.
verses.135:3: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:4: to Him who alone works great wonders, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:5: to Him who made the heavens with understanding, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:6: to Him who made the earth firm upon the water, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:7: to Him who alone made great lights, for His mercy abides forever—
verses.135:8: the sun for dominion over the day, for His mercy abides forever,
verses.135:9: the moon and the stars for dominion over the night, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:10: to Him who struck Egypt together with their firstborn, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:11: and brought Israel out from their midst, for His mercy abides forever,
verses.135:12: with a mighty hand and with an uplifted arm, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:13: to Him who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:14: and led Israel through the midst of it, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:15: and shook off Pharaoh and his host into the Red Sea, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:16: to Him who led His people through the wilderness, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:17: to Him who struck great kings, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:18: and slew mighty kings, for His mercy abides forever—
verses.135:19: Sihon king of the Amorites, for His mercy abides forever,
verses.135:20: and Og king of Bashan, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:21: and gave their land as an inheritance, for His mercy abides forever,
verses.135:22: an inheritance to Israel His servant, for His mercy abides forever.
verses.135:23: For in our lowliness the Lord remembered us, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:24: and redeemed us from the hand of our enemies, for His mercy abides forever;
verses.135:25: He who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy abides forever.
verses.135:26: Give thanks to the Lord of heaven, for His mercy abides forever.
verses.136:1: Of David. By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, and we wept as we remembered Zion.
verses.136:2: Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments.
verses.136:3: For there those who took us captive asked of us words of songs, and those who led us away said, "Sing hymns to us from the songs of Zion."
verses.136:4: How shall we sing the song of the Lord upon a foreign land?
verses.136:5: If I forget you, O Jerusalem, may my right hand be forgotten;
verses.136:6: may my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem foremost at the head of my gladness.
verses.136:7: Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who said, "Empty it, empty it, even to the foundation in it."
verses.136:8: O wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who will repay you the repayment that you repaid to us;
verses.136:9: blessed is he who will seize and dash your infants against the rock.
verses.137:1: Of David. I will give thanks to You, O Lord, with my whole heart, for You have heard the words of my mouth; and before the angels I will sing praises to You.
verses.137:2: I will worship toward Your holy temple, and give thanks to Your name for Your mercy and Your truth; for You have magnified Your holy name above all things.
verses.137:3: In whatever day I call, hear me swiftly; You will greatly care for me in my soul with great strength.
verses.137:4: Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to You, O Lord, for they have heard all the words of Your mouth;
verses.137:5: and let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for the glory of the Lord is great;
verses.137:6: for the Lord is high, and He looks upon the lowly, and the lofty He knows from afar.
verses.137:7: Though I walk in the midst of affliction, You will keep me alive; against the wrath of enemies You stretched out my hands, and Your right hand saved me.
verses.137:8: O Lord, You will recompense on my behalf; O Lord, Your mercy endures forever; O Lord, do not disregard the works of Your hands.
verses.138:1: For the end; a psalm of David. O Lord, You have examined me and known me;
verses.138:2: You know my sitting down and my rising up; You perceive all my thoughts from afar;
verses.138:3: You have traced out my path and my measuring line, and You have foreseen all my ways,
verses.138:4: for there is no unrighteous word on my tongue; behold, O Lord, You have known all things,
verses.138:5: the last things and the ancient things; You fashioned me and laid Your hand upon me.
verses.138:6: Your knowledge has become too wondrous for me; it has grown mighty; I cannot attain to it.
verses.138:7: Where shall I go from Your Spirit? And from Your presence where shall I flee?
verses.138:8: If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I descend into Hades, You are present;
verses.138:9: if I take up my wings straight ahead and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea,
verses.138:10: for even there Your hand shall guide me, and Your right hand shall hold me fast.
verses.138:11: And I said, "Surely darkness shall trample me down, and night shall be illumination in my delight."
verses.138:12: As its darkness is, so also is its light.
verses.138:13: For You possessed my inward parts, O Lord; You upheld me from my mother's womb.
verses.138:14: I will give thanks to You, for You have been fearfully made wondrous; marvelous are Your works, and my soul knows full well.
verses.138:15: My bone was not hidden from You, which You made in secret, nor my substance in the lowest parts of the earth;
verses.138:16: My eyes saw Your unwrought work, and in Your book all shall be written; day by day they shall be fashioned, and there is not one among them.
verses.138:17: But to me Your friends are exceedingly honored, O God; their dominions have grown exceedingly mighty;
verses.138:18: I will count them, and they shall be multiplied more than the sand; I awoke, and I am still with You.
verses.138:19: If only You would slay sinners, O God! Men of blood, depart from me;
verses.138:20: for You will say concerning reasoning, "They shall take Your cities in vain."
verses.138:21: Have I not hated those who hate You, O Lord, and wasted away over Your enemies?
verses.138:22: With a perfect hatred I hated them; they became enemies to me.
verses.138:23: Examine me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my paths;
verses.138:24: and see if You have seen iniquities in me, and guide me in the everlasting way.
verses.139:1: For the end; a psalm of David.
verses.139:2: Deliver me, O Lord, from an evil man; from an unrighteous man rescue me,
verses.139:3: who devised injustices in the heart; all the day long they arrayed battles;
verses.139:4: they sharpened their tongue like that of a serpent; the venom of asps is under their lips. Interlude.
verses.139:5: Keep me, O Lord, from the hand of a sinner; from unrighteous men deliver me, who have plotted to trip up my steps;
verses.139:6: the proud have hidden a snare for me, and stretched out cords, snares for my feet; alongside the path they have set a stumbling block for me. Interlude.
verses.139:7: I said to the Lord, "You are my God"; give ear, O Lord, to the voice of my supplication.
verses.139:8: O Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, You have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.
verses.139:9: Do not deliver me up, O Lord, from my desire to a sinner; they have plotted against me; do not forsake me, lest they ever be exalted. Interlude.
verses.139:10: The head of their encirclement—the toil of their lips shall cover them.
verses.139:11: Coals of fire shall fall upon them on the earth, and You shall cast them down. In miseries they shall by no means endure;
verses.139:12: evils shall hunt down an unrighteous man to destruction.
verses.139:13: I know that the Lord will execute the judgment of the poor and the justice of the needy.
verses.139:14: Surely the righteous shall give thanks to Your name, and the upright shall dwell in Your presence.
verses.140:1: A Psalm of David. O Lord, to You I have cried out; hear me; attend to the voice of my supplication when I cry out to You.
verses.140:2: Let my prayer be directed as incense before You, the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.
verses.140:3: Place a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of enclosure around my lips.
verses.140:4: Do not turn my heart aside to words of wickedness, to devise excuses in sins with men who work lawlessness; and by no means shall I join with their chosen ones.
verses.140:5: A righteous man shall chasten me in mercy and reprove me, but do not let the oil of a sinner anoint my head; for yet again and again my prayer is in their good pleasures.
verses.140:6: Their mighty ones have been swallowed up beside a rock; they shall hear my words, for they have prevailed.
verses.140:7: As a clod of earth is broken apart upon the earth, our bones have been scattered beside Hades.
verses.140:8: For toward You, O Lord, Lord, are my eyes; in You I have put my hope; do not take away my soul.
verses.140:9: Keep me from the snare which they have set for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who work lawlessness.
verses.140:10: Sinners shall fall into his net; I am alone until I pass by.
verses.141:1: Of understanding, of David, when he was in the cave; a prayer.
verses.141:2: With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord.
verses.141:3: I will pour out my supplication before Him; I will declare my affliction in His presence.
verses.141:4: When my spirit failed within me, then You knew my paths; in this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me.
verses.141:5: I looked to the right and watched, for there was no one who recognized me; escape perished from me, and there is no one who cares for my soul.
verses.141:6: To You, O Lord, I cried out, and I said, "You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living."
verses.141:7: Attend to my supplication, for I have been brought exceedingly low; deliver me from those who pursue me, for they have grown stronger than I.
verses.141:8: Bring my soul out of prison, that I may give thanks to Your name, O Lord; the righteous shall wait for me until You reward me.
verses.142:1: A Psalm of David, when his son pursued him. O Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication in Your truth; answer me in Your righteousness.
verses.142:2: And do not enter into judgment with Your servant, for no one living shall be justified in Your sight.
verses.142:3: He has brought my life low to the earth; he has made me dwell in dark places, like the dead of ages past.
verses.142:4: And my spirit grew despondent within me; inside me my heart was troubled.
verses.142:5: I remembered days of old, and I meditated on all Your works; on the deeds of Your hands I pondered.
verses.142:6: I stretched out my hands to You; my soul is like a waterless land before You. Interlude.
verses.142:7: Hear me swiftly, O Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn Your face away from me, lest I become like those who go down into the pit.
verses.142:8: Cause me to hear Your mercy in the morning, for in You I have put my hope; make known to me, O Lord, the way in which I shall walk, for to You I have lifted up my soul.
verses.142:9: Rescue me from my enemies, O Lord, for to You I have fled for refuge.
verses.142:10: Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God; Your Holy Spirit shall guide me in the straight way.
verses.142:11: For the sake of Your name, O Lord, You shall revive me in Your righteousness; You shall bring my soul out of affliction.
verses.142:12: And in Your mercy You shall cut off my enemies, and You shall destroy all those who afflict my soul; for I am Your servant.
verses.143:1: Of David, against Goliath. Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle array, my fingers for war,
verses.143:2: my mercy and my refuge, my protector and my deliverer, my shield—and in Him I have hoped—who subdues my people under me.
verses.143:3: O Lord, what is man, that You were made known to him, or a son of man, that You take account of him?
verses.143:4: Man has been likened to vanity; his days pass by like a shadow.
verses.143:5: O Lord, incline Your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they shall smoke.
verses.143:6: Flash forth lightning, and You shall scatter them; send forth Your arrows, and You shall confound them.
verses.143:7: Send forth Your hand from on high; rescue me and deliver me out of many waters, out of the hand of foreign sons,
verses.143:8: whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of unrighteousness.
verses.143:9: O God, I will sing a new song to You; on a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praises to You,
verses.143:10: who gives salvation to kings, who redeems David His servant. From an evil sword
verses.143:11: deliver me, and rescue me out of the hand of foreign sons, whose mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of unrighteousness;
verses.143:12: whose sons are like young plants grown sturdy in their youth, their daughters beautified, adorned all around after the likeness of a temple;
verses.143:13: their storehouses are full, overflowing from this into that; their sheep bear abundantly, multiplying in their goings out,
verses.143:14: their oxen are fat; there is no collapse of a fence, nor breaking out, nor outcry in their courtyards.
verses.143:15: They called blessed the people to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.
verses.144:1: A Praise of David. I will exalt You, my God, my King, and I will bless Your name forever and ever.
verses.144:2: Every day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name.
verses.144:3: Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised, and to His greatness there is no end.
verses.144:4: Generation after generation shall praise Your works, and they shall proclaim Your power;
verses.144:5: and they shall speak of the majesty of the glory of Your holiness, and they shall recount Your wondrous works;
verses.144:6: and they shall tell of the power of Your awesome deeds, and as for Your greatness, I will recount it; and they shall speak of Your might.
verses.144:7: They shall pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of Your goodness, and in Your righteousness they shall exult.
verses.144:8: Compassionate and merciful is the Lord, longsuffering and abounding in mercy.
verses.144:9: Good is the Lord to those who wait patiently, and His tender mercies are over all His works.
verses.144:10: Let all Your works give thanks to You, O Lord, and let Your devout ones bless You.
verses.144:11: They shall tell of the glory of Your kingdom, and they shall speak of Your might,
verses.144:12: to make known to the sons of men Your might, and the glory of the majesty of Your kingdom.
verses.144:13: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all the ages, and Your dominion is through every generation and generation. Faithful is the Lord in His words, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:14: The Lord upholds all who are falling, and lifts up all who are cast down.
verses.144:15: The eyes of all hope in You, and You give them their food in due season;
verses.144:16: You open Your hands, and fill every living creature with goodwill.
verses.144:17: Righteous is the Lord in all His ways, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:18: Near is the Lord to all who call upon Him, to all who call upon Him in truth.
verses.144:19: He will grant the desire of those who fear Him, and He will hear their supplication and save them.
verses.144:20: The Lord guards all who love Him, and all the sinners He will utterly destroy.
verses.144:21: The praise of the Lord my mouth shall speak, and let all flesh bless His holy name forever and ever.
verses.145:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord, O my soul.
verses.145:2: I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing praises to my God as long as I exist.
verses.145:3: Do not trust in rulers, nor in sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.
verses.145:4: His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return to his earth; in that day all their thoughts shall perish.
verses.145:5: Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God,
verses.145:6: who made the heaven and the earth, the sea and all things that are in them; who guards truth forever,
verses.145:7: who executes justice for those who are wronged, who gives food to the hungry. The Lord looses those who are fettered.
verses.145:8: The Lord lifts up those who are cast down; the Lord makes the blind wise; the Lord loves the righteous.
verses.145:9: The Lord guards the sojourners; He will sustain the orphan and the widow, and the way of sinners He will blot out.
verses.145:10: The Lord shall reign forever, your God, O Zion, from generation to generation.
verses.146:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; may praise be sweet to our God.
verses.146:2: The Lord builds Jerusalem, and He shall gather together the dispersions of Israel—
verses.146:3: He who heals those who are crushed in heart and binds up their wounds,
verses.146:4: He who numbers the multitudes of stars and calls them all by their names.
verses.146:5: Great is our Lord, and great is His might, and of His understanding there is no number.
verses.146:6: The Lord lifts up the meek, but He brings sinners low even to the earth.
verses.146:7: Begin a song to the Lord with thanksgiving; make melody to our God upon the harp,
verses.146:8: to Him who clothes heaven with clouds, who prepares rain for the earth, who causes grass to spring up upon the mountains, and green herbage for the service of men,
verses.146:9: and who gives to the cattle their food, and to the young of the ravens that call upon Him.
verses.146:10: He will not take pleasure in the might of the horse, nor is He well pleased with the legs of a man.
verses.146:11: The Lord is well pleased with those who fear Him, and with all those who hope in His mercy.
verses.147:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Extol the Lord, O Jerusalem; praise your God, O Zion.
verses.147:2: For He has made strong the bars of your gates; He has blessed your sons within you.
verses.147:3: He makes your borders peace, and fills you with the fat of wheat.
verses.147:4: He sends forth His oracle to the earth; His word shall run swiftly.
verses.147:5: He gives snow like wool; He scatters mist like ashes.
verses.147:6: He casts forth His ice like morsels; before the face of His cold, who shall stand?
verses.147:7: He shall send forth His word and melt them; His wind shall blow, and the waters shall flow.
verses.147:8: He proclaims His word to Jacob, His ordinances and His judgments to Israel.
verses.147:9: He has not done thus to any nation, and His judgments He has not made known to them.
verses.148:1: Hallelujah. Of Haggai and Zechariah. Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the highest.
verses.148:2: Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His powers.
verses.148:3: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all the stars and the light.
verses.148:4: Praise Him, O heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens.
verses.148:5: Let them praise the name of the Lord, for He spoke, and they came into being; He commanded, and they were created.
verses.148:6: He established them forever and ever; He set a decree, and it shall not pass away.
verses.148:7: Praise the Lord from the earth: dragons and all deeps;
verses.148:8: fire, hail, snow, ice, wind of the tempest, which perform His word;
verses.148:9: the mountains and all hills, fruit-bearing trees and all cedars;
verses.148:10: wild beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds;
verses.148:11: kings of the earth and all peoples, rulers and all judges of the earth;
verses.148:12: young men and maidens, old men with youths.
verses.148:13: Let them praise the name of the Lord, for His name alone has been exalted; His praise is over earth and heaven.
verses.148:14: And He shall exalt the horn of His people, for the sons of Israel, a people drawing near to Him.
verses.149:1: Hallelujah. Sing to the Lord a new song; His praise is in the congregation of the devout.
verses.149:2: Let Israel be glad in Him who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their King.
verses.149:3: Let them praise His name with dancing; with timbrel and psaltery let them make melody to Him.
verses.149:4: For the Lord is well pleased with His people, and He will exalt the meek with salvation.
verses.149:5: The devout shall exult in glory, and they shall rejoice upon their beds.
verses.149:6: The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands,
verses.149:7: to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples,
verses.149:8: to bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles,
verses.149:9: to carry out upon them the written judgment; this glory belongs to all His devout ones.
verses.150:1: Hallelujah. Praise God in His holy places; praise Him in the firmament of His power.
verses.150:2: Praise Him for His mighty deeds; praise Him according to the abundance of His majesty.
verses.150:3: Praise Him with the blast of the trumpet; praise Him with psaltery and lyre.
verses.150:4: Praise Him with timbrel and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute.
verses.150:5: Praise Him with melodious cymbals; praise Him with cymbals of jubilation.
verses.150:6: Let every breath praise the Lord. Hallelujah.
verses.151:1: This psalm is written by David's own hand and is outside the number, when he fought in single combat with Goliath. I was small among my brethren, and the youngest in the house of my father; I tended the sheep of my father.
verses.151:2: My hands made a musical instrument; my fingers tuned a psaltery.
verses.151:3: And who will declare it to my Lord? The Lord Himself, He Himself hears.
verses.151:4: He Himself sent forth His messenger, and took me from the sheep of my father, and anointed me with the oil of His anointing.
verses.151:5: My brethren were handsome and tall, yet the Lord was not well pleased with them.
verses.151:6: I went forth to meet the foreigner, and he cursed me by his idols;
verses.151:7: but I drew the sword from his side and beheaded him, and took away reproach from the sons of Israel.

notes.1:1: The Greek noun rendered "pestilent men" literally means "plagues" or "pestilences," used figuratively in the Septuagint for corrupt or scornful persons (where the Hebrew text has "scoffers").
notes.1:4: The Septuagint doubles the opening negation ("Not so ... not so") and adds "from the face of the earth," neither of which appears in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.1:5: The Greek reads "counsel" (the same term used in verse 1) rather than "congregation" as in the Hebrew text, reinforcing the contrast between the counsel of the ungodly and the counsel of the righteous.
notes.2:2: The Greek term rendered "Interlude" (diapsalma) denotes a musical pause corresponding to the Hebrew "Selah"; it appears here in the Septuagint though absent in the Hebrew text.
notes.2:6: Unlike the Hebrew text ("I have set My King"), the Septuagint uses the passive voice spoken by the Anointed One ("I was appointed by Him"), and this Greek text omits the word "king."
notes.2:9: The Greek verb means "shepherd" (reflecting an alternate vocalization of the Hebrew consonants, as quoted in Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15) rather than "break" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.2:12: Where the Hebrew text is traditionally rendered "Kiss the Son," the Septuagint reads "Lay hold of instruction," and also specifies "the righteous way" rather than simply "the way."
notes.3:1: In the Septuagint, the psalm superscription is numbered as verse 1, shifting the remaining verse numbers ahead by one compared to most English translations based on the Hebrew text.
notes.3:4: The Greek term means "protector" or "helper" rather than "shield" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.3:8: The Septuagint reads "all who are hostile to me without cause" rather than "all my enemies on the cheekbone" as in the Hebrew text.
notes.4:1: Greek eis to telos ("for the end") is the Septuagint's standard superscription rendering of the Hebrew musical heading often translated "to the choirmaster," giving the psalm a culminating or eschatological sense.
notes.4:3: The Septuagint reads "heavy of heart" (barykardioi) where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "my honor into shame," and marks a musical pause with diapsalma ("Interlude," corresponding to Hebrew selah).
notes.4:7: Greek esemeiothe ("has been marked" or "signed") reflects a reading of the Hebrew verb from the root for "sign" or "banner," rather than the Masoretic "lift up."
notes.4:8: The Septuagint includes "and oil" alongside wheat and wine and reads "from the fruit of" where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "more than in the time when."
notes.5:1: Greek hyper tes kleronomouses ("concerning her who inherits") interprets the Hebrew musical heading (ha-nechiloth, often linked to flutes) from the Hebrew root meaning "to inherit."
notes.5:9: The Septuagint reads "make my way straight before You," reversing the possessive pronouns found in the Masoretic Hebrew ("make Your way straight before my face").
notes.5:12: Greek kataskenoseis en autois ("You shall dwell among them," literally "tabernacle among them") renders the Hebrew verb as dwelling rather than covering or defending.
notes.5:13: The Septuagint ends with the first-person plural "You have crowned us" (hemas), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew has the third-person singular "You surround him."
notes.6:1: Greek hyper tes ogdoes ("concerning the eighth") translates the Hebrew musical term ha-sheminith, variously understood as an eight-stringed instrument, a lower octave, or the eighth day.
notes.6:6: Greek Hades is the Septuagint's regular rendering of Hebrew Sheol (the realm of the dead), and exomologesetai denotes grateful confession or praise.
notes.6:8: Greek thymou ("wrath") renders a Hebrew word for grief or vexation, and epalaiothen ("I have grown old") reads the verb as first-person singular rather than third-person singular referring to the eye.
notes.7:1: The Greek superscription names "Chusi, the son of Jemini," corresponding to "Cush, a Benjamite" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.7:5: The Greek reads "then indeed let me fall away empty from my enemies," whereas the Hebrew text speaks of plundering or rescuing an adversary without cause.
notes.7:6: Greek diapsalma denotes a musical interlude or pause in the psalm, corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.7:12: The Greek includes "strong and longsuffering" and adds the negation "not bringing wrath every day," contrasting with the Hebrew text's "indignant every day."
notes.7:14: Greek tois kaiomenois ("for those who burn") reflects a Hebrew participle that can denote either fiery shafts or hot pursuers.
notes.8:1: The Greek superscription renders the musical heading as "For the end, concerning the winepresses," corresponding to Hebrew lamnatseach al-haggittith.
notes.8:3: The Greek reads "praise" (ainon, as quoted in Matthew 21:16), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "strength."
notes.8:6: The Greek translates Hebrew elohim as "angels" (angelous, quoted in Hebrews 2:7), and brachy ti can mean either "a little" in status or "for a little while" in duration.
notes.9:1: The Greek superscription reads "concerning the hidden things of the son," interpreting the Hebrew musical heading al-muth labben differently from the Masoretic vocalization.
notes.9:17: Greek ode diapsalmatos ("A song of interlude") corresponds to Higgaion Selah in the Hebrew text.
notes.9:21: The Greek reads "a lawgiver" (nomotheten), vocalizing the Hebrew consonantal text as "teacher/lawgiver" rather than "terror."
notes.9:22: From 9:22 through 9:39, the Septuagint continues Psalm 9 as one composition where the Hebrew Masoretic Text begins Psalm 10.
notes.9:36: The Greek concludes with di' auten ("because of it"), indicating that the sinner will disappear on account of his sin when it is sought out.
notes.10:1: The Greek superscription "For the end" (eis to telos) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading, and the Greek reads the plural "mountains" and "sparrow" (strouthion).
notes.10:2: The Greek reads "in a quiver" (eis pharetran) rather than "upon the bowstring," and uses the rare compound skotomene, meaning a dark, moonless night.
notes.10:3: Addressing God directly, the Greek reads "the things You have established, they have torn down" (ha katertiso katheilon), differing from the Hebrew "if the foundations are destroyed."
notes.10:5: Whereas the Hebrew reads that God's soul hates the wicked and the lover of violence, the Greek states that the Lord examines both the righteous and the ungodly, while he who loves unrighteousness hates his own soul.
notes.11:1: "Concerning the eighth" (hyper tes ogdoes) renders the Hebrew musical heading al-hasheminith, often understood as an eight-stringed instrument or octave, or in early Christian interpretation as the eschatological eighth day.
notes.11:3: "With a heart and a heart" literally reproduces the Greek Hebraism (en kardia kai en kardia) denoting a double or duplicitous heart.
notes.11:6: The Greek verbs thesomai ("I will set [him]") and parresiasomai en auto ("I will act boldly on his behalf," or "speak openly concerning him") assume a singular implied object referring to the poor and needy person just named.
notes.11:9: Differing sharply from the Hebrew ("when vileness is exalted among the sons of men"), the Greek reads "according to Your height, You have greatly cared for (epolyoresas) the sons of men."
notes.12:2: In this Greek versification, the superscription and opening questions appear together as verse two, and the Greek asks how long the Lord will "turn Your face away" (apostrepseis) rather than "hide" it.
notes.12:3: The Greek text reads simply "by day" (hemeras), without the expansion "and by night" found in some later Greek witnesses.
notes.12:6: The closing clause, "and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High," is a distinctive Septuagint addition not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.13:1: The Greek superscription "For the end" (eis to telos) renders the Hebrew musical heading often translated "To the choirmaster" and was frequently read in an eschatological sense. Both here and in verse 3, the Septuagint adds "there is not even one."
notes.13:3: The Septuagint includes an extended indictment of human depravity gathered from other scriptural passages (cf. Psalms 5:10; 139:4; 9:28; Isaiah 59:7-8; Psalm 35:2) that is quoted by the apostle Paul in Romans 3:13-18; the Hebrew Masoretic Text ends the verse after "not even one."
notes.13:5: The Septuagint includes the clause "where there was no fear" (paralleling Psalm 52:6 LXX / 53:5 MT), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 14:5.
notes.14:3: The Greek verb edolosen ("dealt deceitfully") reflects a different understanding of the underlying Hebrew than the Masoretic Text's "slanders."
notes.14:4: The Septuagint reads "to his neighbor" (to plesion autou), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's "to his own hurt."
notes.15:1: The Greek superscription stelographia ("pillar inscription") is the Septuagint rendering of the obscure Hebrew musical or literary term miktam.
notes.15:2: The critical Greek text provided here consists solely of "I said to the Lord, 'You are my Lord,'" without the additional clause ("for You have no need of my goods") present in some Septuagint manuscripts and corresponding to the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.15:3: Whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks in the first person of the psalmist's delight in the saints, the Septuagint uses third-person forms ("His land," "He has made wondrous," "His desires"), making the Lord the subject.
notes.15:4: The Septuagint renders the difficult Hebrew as "Their infirmities were multiplied; after these things they hastened" and "gather their assemblies of blood," differing notably from the Masoretic Text's reference to the sorrows of those who hasten after another god and pouring out drink offerings of blood.
notes.15:9: The Septuagint reads "my tongue" (he glossa mou) and "in hope" (ep' elpidi) rather than the Masoretic Text's "my glory" and "in security"; verses 8-11 are quoted in this Greek form in Acts 2:25-28.
notes.16:2: The Greek reads "my eyes" (hoi ophthalmoi mou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Your eyes."
notes.16:4: The Greek reads "hard ways" (hodous skleras) as the difficult path faithfully kept by the psalmist, differing from the Masoretic Text's "paths of the violent."
notes.16:13: The Greek leaves "Your sword" (rhomphaian sou) in the accusative without a separate verb, linking it directly into verse 14.
notes.16:14: The Greek text here reads "dismissing them from the earth" (apolyon apo ges, a manuscript variant alongside "from the few," apo oligon) and "swine's flesh" (hyeion, rather than "sons," huion).
notes.17:3: The Greek renders the opening metaphor as "firmament" (stereoma), emphasizing steadfast solidity and unshakable foundation.
notes.17:21: This Greek text repeats the opening clause of verse 18 ("He will deliver me from my mighty enemies and from those who hate me") at the start of verse 21.
notes.17:30: The Greek reads "I shall be delivered from a marauding band" (rhysthesomai apo peirateriou), differing from the Masoretic Text's "I can run against a troop."
notes.17:36: The Greek contains a doubled statement about God's "discipline" (paideia) setting the psalmist upright and teaching him, whereas the Masoretic Text speaks of God's gentleness.
notes.17:46: The Greek reads "went limping from their paths" (echolanan apo ton tribon auton), differing from the Masoretic Text's "came trembling from their strongholds."
notes.18:5: Greek reads "their sound" (phthongos), which is quoted in Romans 10:18, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "their measuring line."
notes.18:6: The Septuagint reads "In the sun He has set His tabernacle," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "In them He has set a tent for the sun."
notes.18:11: Greek reads "much precious stone" rather than the Masoretic Text's "much fine gold."
notes.18:14: Greek reads "strangers" (allotriōn), reflecting a Hebrew consonantal reading for "strangers" rather than the Masoretic Text's "presumptuous sins."
notes.19:4: "Make your whole burnt offering fat" is a sacrificial idiom for graciously accepting the offering. "Interlude" renders Greek diapsalma, a musical pause corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.19:6: Greek reads "we shall be magnified" (megalynthēsometha, also in verse 8), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "we will set up our banners" here and "we will remember" in verse 8.
notes.19:7: "His anointed" translates Greek ton christon autou, the royal title from which "Christ" is derived.
notes.19:10: The Septuagint includes "Your" with "king" and directs both imperatives to the Lord, whereas the Masoretic Text can be read "O Lord, save! May the King answer us."
notes.20:4: Greek reads "a crown of precious stone" rather than the Masoretic Text's "a crown of pure gold."
notes.20:10: The Septuagint addresses the Lord directly here ("O Lord, in Your wrath You shall confound them"), treating verses 9–14 as a unified address to God, whereas the Masoretic Text shifts to the third person.
notes.20:13: "Make them turn their back" renders the literal idiom "make them a back," meaning to put them to flight. "Among Your remnants" translates Greek en tois periloipois sou, reflecting the Hebrew root for "remnant" rather than the Masoretic Text's "on Your bowstrings."
notes.21:2: Greek includes "give heed to me" (προσχες μοι) and reads "the words of my transgressions" (οι λογοι των παραπτωματων μου), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "the words of my groaning."
notes.21:4: Greek εν αγιοις ("among the holy ones") may also be rendered "in the holy places" (the sanctuary), corresponding to Hebrew "holy one."
notes.21:17: Greek ωρυξαν literally means "they dug" (traditionally rendered "pierced"), representing a famous Septuagint divergence from the Masoretic Hebrew "like a lion."
notes.21:18: Greek has third-person plural "They numbered" (εξηριθμησαν), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads first-person singular "I can count."
notes.21:22: Greek μονοκερωτων literally means "unicorns" (one-horned beasts, rendering Hebrew "wild oxen") and concludes with "my lowliness" (την ταπεινωσιν μου), where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "You have answered me."
notes.22:1: Numbered Psalm 22 in the Septuagint (Psalm 23 in Hebrew and most English Bibles). Greek poimainei is a verb ('shepherds'), followed by 'nothing shall cause me to want.'
notes.22:2: Greek kateskenosen ('made to dwell/encamp') and exethrepsen ('nurtured/reared') are aorist narrative verbs carried through verses 2-4.
notes.22:4: The Greek reads 'in the midst of the shadow of death' (en meso skias thanatou) without the word 'valley,' and plural kaka ('evils').
notes.22:5: Greek methyskon hos kratiston literally reads 'intoxicating/gladdening as the mightiest (or choicest),' reflecting the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew for an overflowing cup.
notes.22:6: The Septuagint reads 'Your mercy' alone (without 'goodness'), uses the forceful verb katadioxetai ('shall pursue'), and renders the closing clause with the articular infinitive 'my dwelling.'
notes.23:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "for the first day of the week" (της μιας σαββατων), reflecting the ancient liturgical use of this psalm on Sunday.
notes.23:4: Greek ελαβεν επι ματαιω την ψυχην αυτου ("received his soul in vain") reflects Septuagint idiom for taking something in vain (cf. Exod 20:7), and adds "to his neighbor" at the close of the verse.
notes.23:6: Greek διαψαλμα ("Interlude") is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew notation Selah; the verse also reads "the God of Jacob."
notes.23:7: Greek αρατε πυλας, οι αρχοντες υμων literally means "Lift up gates, your rulers" (repeated in v. 9), interpreting the Hebrew "heads" as "rulers" or "princes" rather than "Lift up your heads, O gates."
notes.24:8: Greek νομοθετησει ("will give law to," also in v. 12) interprets the Hebrew verb for "instruct" specifically in terms of lawgiving.
notes.24:14: Greek renders Hebrew "counsel" as κραταιωμα ("stronghold") and includes the additional clause "and the name of the Lord belongs to those who fear Him."
notes.24:21: Greek has personal plural subjects "The innocent and the upright clung to me" (ακακοι και ευθεις εκολλωντο μοι) and adds "O Lord," whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads abstract nouns "integrity and uprightness."
notes.25:2: The Greek verb means "refine with fire," and "inward parts" translates Greek nephrous (lit. "kidneys"), representing the seat of one's deepest affections and conscience.
notes.25:3: The Greek reads "I have been well pleased" (euerestesa), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I have walked."
notes.25:6: Greek en athoois is plural, meaning "among the innocent," though some interpreters take it abstractly as "in innocence."
notes.25:7: The Greek uses the active infinitive "to hear" (akousai), in contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text's causative sense, "to proclaim aloud."
notes.26:1: The phrase "before he was anointed" is a distinctive Septuagint addition to the superscription not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.26:6: The Greek reads "I went around" (ekyklosa), interpreting the Hebrew phrase "around me" as a verb, and uses past-tense verbs throughout verses 5 and 6.
notes.26:8: The Greek punctuates "to You my heart has said" as concluding the speech of verse 7, and follows with the first-person "I have earnestly sought" (exezetesa) where the Hebrew has the command "Seek My face."
notes.26:12: "Desires" translates Greek psychas (lit. "souls"); the closing clause "and injustice has lied to itself" is a distinctive Septuagint reading where the Hebrew speaks of breathing out violence.
notes.26:13: The Septuagint omits the opening conditional particle ("Unless...") of the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and the Greek critical text here reads the future tense "I will believe" (pisteuso).
notes.27:1: The Greek addresses God as "O my God," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my rock."
notes.27:5: The Greek shifts to the second person ("You shall tear them down and never build them up"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the third person ("He").
notes.27:7: "My flesh blossomed anew" and "of my own will" are distinctive Septuagint readings where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my heart exults" and "with my song."
notes.27:8: The Greek reads "of His people," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for them"; "salvations" reflects the Greek plural soterion.
notes.28:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "for the closing of the tabernacle," referring to the closing solemn assembly of the Feast of Tabernacles, and preserves a double rendering of the underlying Hebrew as both "sons of God" and "young rams" (literally "sons of rams").
notes.28:6: Following the Septuagint, the Lord "beats them small" rather than making them skip, names "the beloved one" where the Masoretic Hebrew has Sirion, and speaks of "unicorns" (Greek monokeroton, literally one-horned beasts).
notes.28:9: Greek katartizomenou means "strengthens," "prepares," or "brings to fullness," diverging from the Masoretic Hebrew reading "makes the deer give birth."
notes.29:1: "To the end" (Greek Eis to telos) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading often translated "To the choirmaster."
notes.29:6: The Septuagint reads "wrath is in His anger," differing from the Masoretic Hebrew "His anger is but for a moment."
notes.29:8: The Greek text uses the imperative paraschou ("grant") and the noun kallei ("to my beauty"), where the Masoretic Hebrew reads "You made my mountain stand strong."
notes.29:13: Greek katanygo means "be pierced with sorrow" or "feel compunction," corresponding to the Masoretic Hebrew "be silent."
notes.30:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "of alarm" (Greek ekstaseos, also translated "astonishment" or "ecstasy"), echoing the psalmist's cry "in my alarm" in verse twenty-three.
notes.30:7: The Septuagint has the second-person verb "You have hated" (Greek emisesas), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads first-person "I hate."
notes.30:11: Greek en ptochia ("in poverty") reflects a different reading of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic text's "because of my iniquity."
notes.30:16: The Septuagint reads "my lots" (Greek hoi kleroi mou, meaning one's appointed portions or destiny), where the Masoretic Hebrew has "my times."
notes.30:23: The Septuagint joins the clauses with "Therefore" (Greek dia touto) rather than "Yet" or "Nevertheless," presenting the Lord's hearing as the direct response to the psalmist's alarmed plea.
notes.31:2: The Greek reads "in his mouth" (en to stomati autou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in his spirit."
notes.31:4: The Greek reads "I was turned into misery while a thorn was driven in," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's imagery of summer drought. "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, corresponding to Hebrew selah.
notes.31:5: The Greek reads "the ungodliness of my heart" (tes kardias mou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the guilt of my sin."
notes.31:9: The Greek verb form anxai functions here as an imperatival infinitive ("constrain"), and "to you" (pros se) refers to the addressee of verse eight as the animals' master, though some readers take it as addressed to God.
notes.32:5: The Greek reads "mercy" (eleemosynen) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "righteousness."
notes.32:7: The Greek reads "as in a waterskin" (hos askon), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text's "as a heap."
notes.32:9: The Greek uses plural passive verbs ("they came into being... they were created"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses singular verbs.
notes.32:10: The Greek preserves a third parallel clause, "and sets aside the counsels of rulers," which is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.32:15: The Greek phrase kata monas ("one by one" or "individually") contrasts with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "all together."
notes.33:3: The Greek passive verb epainesthesetai ("shall be praised") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's reflexive sense ("shall make its boast").
notes.33:5: The Greek reads "my sojournings" (paroikion mou), interpreting the Hebrew root in the sense of "sojourn" rather than "terror" or "fear" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.33:6: The Greek uses plural imperatives ("Draw near... and be enlightened"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has third-person past verbs ("They looked... and were radiant").
notes.33:11: The Greek reads "the rich" (plousioi) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "young lions," and adds diapsalma ("Interlude") at the close of the verse.
notes.34:3: Greek "Pour out a sword and shut the way" preserves the Septuagint's literal rendering of the Hebrew imperatives for drawing a weapon and barring the path, taking the second verb as "close/shut" rather than a noun for a weapon.
notes.34:7: The Septuagint reads "the destruction of their snare" (taking the Hebrew noun for "pit" in its sense of destruction/corruption) and "reproached" (reading the Hebrew root for shame/reproach rather than "dug").
notes.34:15: The Septuagint reads "scourges" and two passive verbs, "they were torn apart and felt no remorse," reflecting a different vocalization and interpretation from the Masoretic Text.
notes.34:20: Unlike the Masoretic Text ("they do not speak peace"), the Septuagint reads "to me they spoke words of peace, yet in wrath they plotted deceits," contrasting deceptive peaceful speech with inward hostility.
notes.35:1: "For the end" is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew liturgical heading, understood in Greek tradition as pointing toward fulfillment or consummation.
notes.35:3: The Greek phrase rendered "in his own sight" may alternatively be read as "before Him" (referring to God), and the following infinitive clause ("to discover his iniquity and to hate it") preserves the compact and debated syntax of the source text.
notes.35:8: The Septuagint reads "as You have multiplied Your mercy," linked syntactically to the end of verse seven (though the opening particle may also be read exclamatorily as "How You have multiplied..."), where the Masoretic Text has "How precious is your steadfast love."
notes.36:3: The Septuagint reads a passive verb ("you shall be shepherded") and "upon its wealth," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "feed on faithfulness."
notes.36:20: The Septuagint renders this clause as "at the very moment they are glorified and exalted," differing from the Masoretic Text's "like the splendor of the pastures."
notes.36:22: The Greek uses active participles ("those who bless Him ... those who curse Him," referring to the Lord, though the pronoun could also refer to the righteous one of verse 21), whereas the Masoretic Text has passives ("those blessed/cursed by Him").
notes.36:28: The clause "the blameless shall be avenged" in the Greek critical text corresponds to the missing ayin-line of the Hebrew acrostic; some Greek manuscripts instead read "the lawless shall be driven out."
notes.36:35: The Septuagint specifies "like the cedars of Lebanon," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "like a native green tree."
notes.37:1: The liturgical phrase "concerning the Sabbath" is distinctive to the Septuagint superscription and is absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.37:8: The Greek critical text reads "my soul has been filled with mockeries" (some manuscripts read "loins" instead of "soul"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "my loins are filled with burning."
notes.37:18: The Septuagint renders the noun as "scourges," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "ready to stumble" or "halting."
notes.38:6: Greek palaias literally means "old" (whereas the Hebrew reads "handbreadths," possibly echoed by Greek palaiste, "handbreadth"). "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a musical or liturgical pause corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.38:9: The Greek uses the indicative "You have made me" (edokas me) rather than the negative petition ("do not make me") found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.38:12: Greek hos arakhnen ("like a spider," or possibly "like a spider's web") and "his soul" (ten psykhen autou) reflect a distinct Septuagint reading compared with the Hebrew "like a moth what he treasures."
notes.38:13: The Greek text reads "in the earth" (en te ge), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "with You."
notes.39:7: The Septuagint reads "You have prepared a body for me" (soma de katertiso moi) rather than the Hebrew "ears You have dug for me"; this Greek wording is cited in Hebrews 10:5.
notes.39:11: Following the punctuation and reading of the Greek text, "my righteousness" (ten dikaiosynen mou) is the direct object of "O Lord, You have known" at the end of verse 10, followed by "I have not hidden Your truth in my heart."
notes.39:12: Greek antelabonto is an aorist indicative ("have continually upheld me"), affirming God's ongoing help rather than expressing a petition as in the Hebrew.
notes.40:3: This Greek text uses optative verbs expressing a blessing and does not include the clause "and keep him alive" found in the Hebrew and some Greek witnesses.
notes.40:8: In the Greek text, "together against me" (epi to auto kat' emou) completes the clause begun at the end of verse 7 ("he went outside and spoke").
notes.40:9: The Greek frames the enemies' taunt as a rhetorical question ("Will he who sleeps not rise up again?", literally "add to rise up"), contrasting with the declarative statement in the Hebrew.
notes.40:10: Greek pternismon ("supplanting" or "tripping up by the heel") renders the Hebrew idiom of lifting the heel in betrayal (compare John 13:18).
notes.40:14: Greek genoito, genoito ("so be it, so be it") renders the closing liturgical "Amen and Amen" at the end of Book I of the Psalms.
notes.41:1: Greek Psalm 41 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 42; "For the end" (eis to telos) is the characteristic Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription.
notes.41:7: "Hermoniim" preserves the Septuagint's plural form of Hermon (Hermonieim), and "from a small mountain" renders the Greek literally (apo orous mikrou), where the Hebrew tradition takes the term as a proper name ("Mount Mizar").
notes.41:9: The Greek text reads "and by night He will declare it" (kai nyktos delosei), differing from traditions that read "His song is with me."
notes.41:11: "In the crushing of my bones" renders the Greek verb katathlasai ("to crush" or "shatter"), conveying deep inward torment amid the taunts of enemies.
notes.42:1: Greek Psalm 42 (Hebrew Psalm 43) includes the superscription "A Psalm of David," which does not appear in the Masoretic Hebrew text.
notes.42:3: The Septuagint translates both verbs as past aorists ("they have guided me and brought me"), rather than jussive petitions ("let them lead me and bring me") as in the Hebrew.
notes.42:4: The Greek addresses "O Lord my God" (Kyrie ho theos mou), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "O God, my God."
notes.43:9: "Interlude" translates the Greek musical term diapsalma (corresponding to Hebrew selah), and "we shall be praised" preserves the Greek passive voice (epainesthesometha).
notes.43:13: "In their shoutings" renders the Septuagint's alalagmasin ("shoutings" or "battle cries"), differing from the Masoretic Hebrew reading "in their prices."
notes.43:19: The Greek text has a second-person singular verb ("yet You turned aside our paths"), contrasting with the Hebrew reading that states the people's own steps had not turned aside.
notes.43:20: "In a place of affliction" translates the Septuagint reading en topo kakoseos, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in a place of jackals."
notes.43:25: "Our poverty" reflects the Septuagint reading tes ptochias hemon, whereas the Hebrew reads "our affliction."
notes.44:1: The Greek phrase rendered "concerning those who shall be changed" reflects the Septuagint translation of the Hebrew superscription term shoshannim ("lilies") from a verbal root meaning "to change," while "For the end" is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading.
notes.44:5: The imperative enteinon literally means "stretch tight" or "draw," commonly used in the Septuagint for bending a bow (or by extension pressing forward), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonantal text.
notes.44:14: The reading "Heshbon" (Esebon) is a notable textual variant found in major Septuagint uncial manuscripts such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, whereas other Greek manuscripts read esothen ("within"), matching the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.44:18: The Greek text here reads the third-person plural mnesthesontai ("They shall remember"), whereas other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew text read first-person singular ("I will cause Your name to be remembered").
notes.45:1: The phrase "concerning hidden things" (hyper ton kryphion) reflects the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical term alamoth from a root meaning "to hide" or "conceal."
notes.45:2: The Greek active participle "that have found us exceedingly" takes "tribulations" as its subject overtaking the psalmist, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of God as "a very present help."
notes.45:6: The reading "with His countenance" (to prosopo) is preserved in major Septuagint uncials including Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, whereas other Greek witnesses read to pros proi ("at the break of dawn"), aligning with the Hebrew.
notes.45:10: The Septuagint reads thyreous ("shields," referring to large oblong shields), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "chariots."
notes.46:5: The Septuagint reads "His inheritance" (ten kleronomian autou) rather than the Hebrew "our inheritance," and renders Hebrew ga'on ("majesty/pride") as kallone ("beauty").
notes.46:10: The Septuagint reads "with the God of Abraham" (reflecting Hebrew 'im "with" rather than 'am "people") and uses a plural verb ("have been exceedingly exalted") whose subject is "God's mighty ones of the earth," whereas the Hebrew has a singular verb referring to God.
notes.47:1: The Greek phrase "for the second day of the week" (literally "of the Sabbath") is a Septuagint liturgical heading designating this psalm for Monday.
notes.47:3: The Septuagint reads "well-rooted" (eurizo) and plural "mountains of Zion," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "beautiful in elevation, Mount Zion."
notes.47:10: The Septuagint reads "in the midst of Your people" (tou laou sou) rather than "in the midst of Your temple" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.47:13: The Greek verb diegesasthe with en ("tell of it among her towers") renders the Hebrew consonantal verb as "recount" rather than "count."
notes.47:15: This critical Greek text concludes at "forever and ever," without the closing clause ("He will guide us") found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some later Greek manuscripts.
notes.48:1: "To the end" (eis to telos) is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical superscription often translated "To the choirmaster."
notes.48:6: "The iniquity of my heel" translates the Greek literally, reflecting a reading of the Hebrew consonantal text often understood in the Masoretic tradition as "my supplanters," and connects loosely to the nominative participle in verse 7.
notes.48:8: The Septuagint reads "a brother" (adelphos), interpreting the Hebrew consonants ach as "brother" rather than the emphatic particle "surely."
notes.48:12: "Their tombs" (hoi taphoi auton) reflects a Hebrew source reading qibram ("their grave") rather than the Masoretic Text's qirbam ("their inward thought").
notes.48:19: The Septuagint addresses God in the second person ("he will give thanks to You when You do good to him"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text addresses the prosperous man.
notes.49:5: The Septuagint uses third-person pronouns ("Gather to Him His holy ones"), continuing the heraldic summons rather than shifting into first-person divine speech as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.49:10: The Septuagint reads "and the oxen" (kai boes), and in verse 11 "birds of heaven" and "beauty of the field," differing from the Masoretic Text ("a thousand hills," "of the mountains," and "all that moves in the field").
notes.49:21: "You supposed lawlessness" translates the Greek literally (hupelabes anomian), where the Septuagint supplies an explicit noun for iniquity in rendering the Hebrew idiom.
notes.49:23: "And there is the way" (kai ekei hodos) reflects the Septuagint reading of the Hebrew consonants as "and there is a way" rather than the Masoretic "and to him who orders his way."
notes.50:6: The Greek passive "when You are judged" (quoted in Romans 3:4) reflects the Septuagint reading, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the active "when You judge."
notes.50:8: The Septuagint reads "the unseen and hidden things of Your wisdom," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of truth in the inward parts and wisdom in the hidden part.
notes.50:14: Greek hegemoniko ("governing" or "guiding") denotes a ruling, directing spirit, differing from the Hebrew "willing spirit."
notes.50:17: In the Greek text, the vocative "O Lord" begins verse 17 to close the clause from verse 16, followed by the future indicative "You shall open my lips."
notes.51:2: The Septuagint genuinely reads "Abimelech" here, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Ahimelech."
notes.51:3: The Septuagint reads "of iniquity all day long" as a further object of the mighty man's boasting, contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "the steadfast love of God endures all the day."
notes.51:5: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical or liturgical term Selah.
notes.52:1: "Maeleth" transliterates the Greek musical or liturgical term maeleth (corresponding to Hebrew Mahalath).
notes.52:6: The Septuagint reads "the bones of those who please men" (Greek anthropareskon), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the bones of him who encamps against you."
notes.53:1: Psalm 53 in the Septuagint corresponds to Psalm 54 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text. "For the end" translates the Greek superscription "eis to telos," and "of understanding" renders "syneseos."
notes.53:5: "Pause" translates the Greek "diapsalma," a musical interlude corresponding to the Hebrew "Selah."
notes.53:8: The Greek text reads "I will give thanks to Your name, for it is good," without the vocative "O Lord" present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.54:9: Following the Greek text, this verse reads "I awaited Him who saves me from faintheartedness and tempest," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest."
notes.54:15: The Greek "edesmata" ("meals" or "foods") reflects an understanding of shared table fellowship, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "sweet counsel."
notes.54:19: "For among many they were with me" preserves the literal Greek phrasing ("en pollois esan syn emoi"), denoting numerous adversaries contending with the psalmist.
notes.54:21: In the Greek text, God stretches forth His hand in recompense ("en to apodidonai") because the wicked profaned His covenant (plural), and the pronoun referent shifts back to the treacherous companion in the second half of 54:22 ("his heart," "his words").
notes.55:1: "The foreigners" translates Greek "hoi allophyloi," the standard Septuagint term for the Philistines; "pillar inscription" translates "stelographian," the Greek rendering of Hebrew "miktam."
notes.55:3: The Greek text places "from the height of the day" ("apo hypsous hemeras") here and links "for many who make war against me" directly to the third-person plural verb "shall be afraid" ("phobethesontai") in 55:4.
notes.55:7: The Greek text reads first-person singular "just as I waited in my soul" ("kathaper hypemeina te psyche mou"), differing from the third-person plural ("they waited for my soul") in some witnesses and the Hebrew.
notes.55:8: "For nothingness will You save them?" renders the Greek "hyper tou methenos soseis autous" as a rhetorical question, reflecting an emphatic denial that God will rescue the wicked.
notes.55:9: The Greek reads "my life," "before You," and "in Your promise," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my wanderings," "in Your bottle," and "in Your book."
notes.56:1: Greek "for a pillar inscription" (stelographia) renders the Hebrew heading term miktam; this psalm corresponds to Psalm 57 in the Hebrew Masoretic numbering.
notes.56:3: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a musical pause or instrumental break corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.56:9: The Greek uses the passive future with a temporal genitive ("I will awaken at dawn"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("I will awaken the dawn").
notes.57:5: Greek thymos ("fury" or "wrath") reflects the dual sense of the underlying Hebrew term for both "wrath" and "venom."
notes.57:6: Literally "nor of a charm prepared by a wise man," rendering Greek pharmakou pharmakeuomenou para sophou.
notes.57:9: The Greek reads "wax that melts" and "fire fell," differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which speaks of a melting snail and the untimely birth of a woman.
notes.57:10: The Greek literally reads "before your thorns understand the bramble," interpreting the difficult Hebrew imagery of pots feeling the heat of burning thorns as a metaphor of swift judgment.
notes.58:5: The Greek uses first-person singular verbs ("I ran and kept a straight course"), affirming the psalmist's innocence, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses third-person plural verbs referring to the enemies.
notes.58:12: The Greek reads "lest they forget Your law" (tou nomou sou), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "lest my people forget."
notes.58:14: The Greek construes "of Jacob" with "God" ("the God of Jacob rules over the ends of the earth"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "God rules in Jacob to the ends of the earth."
notes.58:16: The Greek text here has no negative particle ("if they are satisfied, they shall also murmur"), depicting chronic discontent even when fed; the Hebrew Masoretic Text and some Greek manuscripts read "if they are not satisfied."
notes.59:1: The Greek superscription renders the Hebrew heading terms as "For the end" (eis to telos), "for those who shall be changed" (tois alloioothesomenois), and "a pillar inscription" (stelographian).
notes.59:2: The Greek reads "set fire to" (enepyrisen) and preserves the distinct proper name Sobal (Sobal, corresponding to Hebrew Zobah), followed by "struck the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand."
notes.59:3: The Greek uses the aorist indicative "You had compassion on us" (oikteiresas hemas), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has an imperative plea ("restore us").
notes.59:6: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a liturgical marker for a musical pause; the Greek also reads "that they may flee from before the bow" (tou phygein apo prosopou toxou).
notes.59:10: The Greek reads "cauldron of My hope" (lebes tes elpidos mou), uses Idumea (Idoumaia) for Edom, and has "to Me the foreigners have been subjected" (emoi allophyloi hypetagesan).
notes.60:2: The Greek text opens the petition directly without the vocative "O God."
notes.60:3: The Greek uses past-tense indicatives ("You lifted me up, You guided me") rather than the imperative prayer found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.60:8: The Greek frames the second clause as a rhetorical question ("who will seek them out?"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads an imperative ("appoint mercy and truth").
notes.61:2: The Greek opens with a rhetorical question using "be subject to God" (hypotagesetai), contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's declarative "Truly my soul waits in silence."
notes.61:5: The Greek reads "they ran in thirst" (edramon en dipsei), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("they delight in lies").
notes.61:9: The Greek "every congregation of people" (pasa synagoge laou) reflects a different reading of the Hebrew consonants rendered "at all times" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.62:1: The Septuagint reads "Idumea" (Edom), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Judah."
notes.62:2: Greek "posaplos" ("how manifoldly") reflects the Septuagint reading the Hebrew verb for "yearns" or "faints" as the interrogative "how many times."
notes.62:3: The Greek passive "I appeared before You" differs from the Masoretic Text's active "I have looked upon You."
notes.62:7: The Septuagint reads "at my dawn" ("en to orthro mou"), whereas the Masoretic Text has "in the night watches."
notes.63:1: "For the end" ("eis to telos") is the standard Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew superscription often translated "To the Chief Musician."
notes.63:7: Greek "a man shall draw near, and a deep heart" reflects the Septuagint taking the Hebrew noun for "inward part" as a verb meaning "to draw near."
notes.63:8: The Septuagint reads "and God shall be exalted. Their blows have become the arrow of infants," whereas the Masoretic Text states that God shoots them with an arrow and they are suddenly wounded.
notes.64:2: Greek "is fitting" ("prepei") differs from the Masoretic Text's "awaits" or "silence," and this Greek text ends with "a vow shall be paid" without adding "in Jerusalem."
notes.64:6: The Greek links "wondrous in righteousness" to "Your temple" in the preceding verse and omits the Masoretic Text's phrase concerning the distant seas.
notes.64:8: The Septuagint reads "who stirs up" ("ho syntarasson") the water of the sea, contrasting with the Masoretic Text's "who stills" the roaring of the seas.
notes.64:14: Greek "The rams of the sheep" translates a Hebrew term that can mean either "rams" or "pastures," producing "The rams of the sheep have clothed themselves" rather than "The pastures are clothed with flocks."
notes.65:1: The Septuagint superscription adds ἀναστάσεως ("of resurrection"), which is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.65:4: "Interlude" translates Greek διάψαλμα, indicating a musical pause or interlude corresponding to the Hebrew Selah.
notes.65:7: The Greek critical text reads ἐν τῇ δυναστίᾳ τοῦ αἰῶνος αὐτοῦ ("by the dominion of His eternity"), differing from manuscripts that read "by His dominion forever."
notes.65:11: The Greek critical text reads ἐνώπιον ἡμῶν ("before us"), where other Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew text read "upon our back."
notes.66:4: The Greek text omits σοι ("to You") in this verse, whereas it includes σοι in the matching refrain at 66:6.
notes.66:7: The aorist ἔδωκεν ("has yielded") expresses thanksgiving for a harvest already granted.
notes.67:5: Greek ἐπὶ δυσμῶν ("upon the west") reflects the Septuagint rendering of a Hebrew term that other traditions translate as "clouds" or "deserts."
notes.67:13: The doubled phrase τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ, τοῦ ἀγαπητοῦ ("of the beloved, of the beloved") reflects the Septuagint reading of a repeated Hebrew verb as a noun from the root meaning "beloved."
notes.67:16: Both ὄρος πῖον ("a rich mountain") and ὄρος τετυρωμένον ("a curdled mountain") are distinctive Septuagint renderings of the Hebrew descriptions of Mount Bashan.
notes.67:19: The closing clause καὶ γὰρ ἀπειθοῦντες τοῦ κατασκηνῶσαι ("indeed, even for the disobedient to dwell") is syntactically elliptical in Greek, while Κύριος ὁ θεός ("the Lord God") opens verse 20 in this critical text.
notes.67:31: The Septuagint renders this difficult clause as a purpose phrase, τοῦ μὴ ἀποκλεισθῆναι τοὺς δεδοκιμασμένους τῷ ἀργυρίῳ ("so that those who are tested with silver may not be shut out").
notes.67:36: The Greek critical text reads ἐν τοῖς ὁσίοις αὐτοῦ ("among His devout ones"), whereas many Septuagint manuscripts read ἐν τοῖς ἁγίοις αὐτοῦ ("among His holy ones").
notes.68:1: The Septuagint superscription reads "concerning those who shall be changed," rendering the Hebrew musical term usually translated "according to Lilies."
notes.68:4: The Greek text reads "from drawing near to my God" (eggizein), a notable textual variant alongside the more widespread Septuagint reading "from hoping in my God" (elpizein).
notes.68:10: The Greek text uses the future tense "shall consume me," matching the quotation in John 2:17, rather than the past tense found in the Hebrew and some Septuagint witnesses.
notes.68:18: The Greek text preserves only this brief petition, omitting the preceding clause ("do not turn away Your face from Your servant") found in the Hebrew and other Septuagint manuscripts.
notes.68:21: The Septuagint reads "my soul expected reproach and misery," taking the Hebrew verb usually rendered "reproach has broken my heart" in the sense of waiting or expecting.
notes.69:1: The Septuagint expands the superscription with the clause "that the Lord may save me," which is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.69:2: The Greek text consists solely of the opening plea, omitting the second clause ("O Lord, make haste to help me") found in the Hebrew and other Septuagint witnesses.
notes.70:1: The Septuagint supplies a superscription linking the psalm to David, the sons of Jonadab, and the first captives, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has no title.
notes.70:12: The Greek text preserves only the opening petition, omitting the second clause ("my God, make haste to help me") found in the Hebrew and other Septuagint witnesses.
notes.70:15: The Greek text reads "business dealings" (pragmatias), differing both from the Septuagint variant "writings/learning" (grammateias) and the Hebrew "numbers."
notes.70:21: The Greek text connects directly to verse 20 with the participle "multiplying" and repeats the closing clause "and from the depths You brought me up again," preserving a distinctive early manuscript reading.
notes.71:4: The Greek places "In righteousness" at the beginning of verse 4 and shifts briefly to the second person ("You will save") between third-person verbs referring to the king.
notes.71:9: The Greek reads "Ethiopians" (Aithiopes) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "desert dwellers."
notes.71:14: The Greek reads "usury" (tokou) and "their name" (to onoma auton) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "oppression" and "their blood."
notes.71:20: The Greek reads "the hymns" (hoi hymnoi) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the prayers."
notes.72:4: The Greek phrasing "no respite in their death, and firmness in their scourge" (ananeusis ... stereoma en te mastigi auton) reflects a distinctive Septuagint rendering that differs markedly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.72:18: The Greek reads "because of their deceits" rather than "in slippery places," and the critical text here consists of this single clause without the additional line about casting them down to ruin.
notes.72:20: The Greek reads "in Your city" (en te polei sou) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "when You awake."
notes.72:21: The Greek reads "my heart was gladdened" (euphranthe) rather than "was embittered"; "inward parts" renders the literal Greek "my kidneys" (hoi nephroi mou).
notes.72:28: The Greek adds the closing phrase "in the gates of the daughter of Zion," which does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.73:9: The Greek reads "and He will know us no more" (kai hemas ou gnosetai eti) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "nor is there any among us who knows how long."
notes.73:14: The Greek text here consists solely of this clause (without the line about crushing the heads of Leviathan) and renders the recipients as "the Ethiopian peoples" (laois tois Aithiopsin).
notes.73:15: The Greek text here preserves only the opening clause about breaking open springs and torrents, without the additional clause about drying up rivers.
notes.73:23: The Greek reads "Your suppliants" (ton hiketon sou) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Your adversaries."
notes.74:1: The Greek superscription "For the end" (eis to telos) renders the Hebrew musical heading often translated "To the chief musician," and "do not destroy" translates the Hebrew tune title Al-tashcheth.
notes.74:2: The Greek text reads "and call upon Your name," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "for Your name is near." In the punctuation of the Greek text, "when I take an appointed time" (v. 3) may conclude this sentence or introduce the divine declaration of judgment that follows.
notes.74:4: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, which corresponds to the Hebrew musical term Selah.
