notes.74:7: The clause is elliptical in Greek (implying "does exaltation come"); "the east" renders Greek exodon ("goings forth," i.e., sunrisings), and this Greek text lacks the word "mountains" found after "deserts" in some manuscripts and the Masoretic Text.
notes.75:1: The Greek superscription adds "concerning the Assyrian," a historical heading absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text that links the psalm to the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib.
notes.75:3: The Greek renders Hebrew be-Shalem ("in Salem") as "in peace" (en eirene).
notes.75:4: This Greek text includes the additional final clause "there He will break the horns" (echoing 74:11), which is absent from the Masoretic Text and some Septuagint manuscripts.
notes.75:9: The Greek text reads ekontisas ("You hurled forth," as with a javelin), a notable early manuscript reading alongside the variant ekoutisas ("You caused to be heard").
notes.75:11: The Greek reads "the thought of man shall give thanks to You, and the remnant of thought shall keep a feast to You," differing markedly from the Masoretic Text's reference to human wrath.
notes.76:3: The Greek reads "and I was not deceived" (ouk epatethen), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "without growing weary."
notes.76:5: This Greek text reads "my enemies" (hoi echthroi mou) rather than the variant "my eyes" (hoi ophthalmoi mou) found in other Septuagint manuscripts and the Masoretic Text.
notes.76:11: The Greek reads "Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High," interpreting the Hebrew consonantal text differently from the Masoretic tradition.
notes.76:19: "In the wheel" (en to trocho) literally translates the Greek rendering of Hebrew baggalgal (often understood as "whirlwind"); this Greek text also lacks the clause "Your lightnings lit up the world" found in other manuscripts.
notes.77:12: The Greek uses Tanis, the Hellenistic name for the Egyptian city of Zoan in the eastern Nile Delta.
notes.77:13: The Greek askos means "waterskin" or "wineskin," reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew from the Masoretic reading "heap."
notes.77:21: The Greek anebaleto literally means "delayed" or "held back," differing from the Masoretic Text's "was full of wrath."
notes.77:31: The Greek phrase "among the greater part of them" (en tois pleiosin auton) corresponds to the Masoretic "among their stoutest men," and "fettered" (synepodisen) literally means "bound the feet of."
notes.77:36: The Greek reads "loved Him" (egapesan auton), whereas the Masoretic Text has "flattered Him"; the clause continues directly into verse 37.
notes.77:46: The Greek erysibe means "blight" or "mildew," differing from the Masoretic Text's "caterpillar."
notes.77:63: The Greek reads "did not mourn" (ouk epenthesan) and in verse 64 uses a passive ("shall not be wept for"), whereas the Masoretic Text speaks of virgins having no wedding songs and widows making no lamentation.
notes.77:65: The Greek participle kekraipalekos (completed by "from wine" in verse 66) denotes being heavy-headed or stuporous from wine, contrasting with the Masoretic "shouting because of wine."
notes.77:69: The Greek hos monokeroton literally means "like [that] of unicorns," arising from reading the Hebrew consonants as re'emim ("wild oxen/unicorns") rather than the Masoretic ramim ("heights").
notes.78:1: Greek oporophylakion means a fruit-watcher's hut or orchard shed, rendering the Hebrew term for heaps of ruins as an image of stark desolation.
notes.78:10: Greek me pote literally reads 'Lest they say,' whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads 'Why should they say.'
notes.78:11: Greek ton tethanatomenon reads 'of those put to death,' whereas the Masoretic Hebrew refers to those appointed to die.
notes.79:1: The Septuagint superscription reads 'concerning those who shall be changed' (interpreting Hebrew Shoshannim, 'lilies') and adds 'concerning the Assyrian,' which does not appear in the Masoretic Text.
notes.79:5: Greek reads the singular 'Your servant,' whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads 'Your people.'
notes.79:8: Greek diapsalma denotes a musical pause or interlude, corresponding to the Hebrew Selah.
notes.79:14: Greek onos agrios reads 'a wild donkey,' differing from the Masoretic Hebrew phrase for creatures moving in the field.
notes.80:1: Greek hyper ton lenon ('concerning the winepresses') interprets the Hebrew term Gittith by connecting it with gath ('winepress').
notes.80:4: Greek eusemo ('notable' or 'distinguished') renders the Hebrew term commonly understood as the full moon.
notes.80:7: Greek edouleusan ('served' or 'labored') depicts Israel's servitude at the basket, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew speaks of hands being freed from the basket.
notes.80:8: Greek Antilogias ('Contradiction' or 'Strife') translates the Hebrew place name Meribah; Greek diapsalma ('Interlude') corresponds to Hebrew Selah.
notes.81:1: The Greek reads "assembly of gods" and makes "gods" the direct object of "judges," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "congregation of the mighty" and "in the midst of the gods He judges."
notes.81:2: Greek diapsalma is the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew selah, denoting a musical pause or interlude, and is translated "Interlude" throughout.
notes.82:2: The Greek reads "who shall be likened to You?" rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "do not keep silent."
notes.82:4: The Greek reads "Your holy ones," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Your treasured ones" or "Your sheltered ones."
notes.82:8: This Greek text reads the proper name "Naibal," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and other Greek manuscripts read "Gebal." Greek allophyloi ("foreigners") is the Septuagint's standard term for the Philistines.
notes.82:13: This Greek text reads "the altar of God," whereas other Greek manuscripts read "the sanctuary of God" and the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the pastures" or "habitations of God."
notes.83:1: "For the end" is the standard Septuagint superscription corresponding to the Hebrew dedication to the choirmaster, and "concerning the winepresses" renders the Hebrew term al-haggittit by associating it with the word for winepress.
notes.83:7: The Greek translates the Hebrew place name Baca as "weeping" and renders the Hebrew term for early rain (moreh) as "the Lawgiver."
notes.83:11: Greek pararripteisthai ("to be cast aside") renders the Hebrew verb for standing at the threshold, and "thousands" is plural in the Greek.
notes.83:12: The Greek reads "the Lord God loves mercy and truth," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the LORD God is a sun and shield."
notes.84:3: Greek diapsalma denotes a musical interlude or pause in psalmody, corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.84:7: The Greek reads as a confident declaration ("You will turn and give us life") rather than the rhetorical question found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.84:8: This Greek text repeats the vocative "O Lord" in the second clause and uses the optative mood ("may You grant").
notes.84:9: The Septuagint reads "and to those who turn their heart toward Him," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text warns against turning back to folly.
notes.85:7: The Greek uses past-tense verbs ("I cried out... You heard me"), recalling answered prayer rather than the future tense found in renderings of the Hebrew text.
notes.85:10: This Greek text concludes with the emphatic epithet "the great [God]" (ho megas) following "You alone are God."
notes.85:11: The Septuagint reads "let my heart rejoice," reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonantal root rendered "unite my heart" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.85:14: Greek paranomoi ("lawless men") and krataion ("mighty men") correspond to "proud" and "violent" men in the Hebrew tradition.
notes.86:1: The masculine pronoun autou ("His") refers to the Lord named in verse two, whereas the feminine pronouns in verses five and six refer to Zion.
notes.86:4: Greek allophyloi (literally "foreigners") is the standard Septuagint rendering for the Philistines.
notes.86:5: The Septuagint reads "Mother Zion" rather than "of Zion" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text; the capitalization of "Man" reflects the Greek source's traditional Christological reading.
notes.86:6: The Greek adds "and of princes" in the Lord's register, a phrase not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.86:7: The Septuagint reads "the dwelling" of "all who rejoice," diverging from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "singers and players... all my springs."
notes.87:1: The superscription preserves the Septuagint phrasing "for the end" (Greek eis to telos), the transliterated musical term "Mahalath" (maeleth), and the Greek gentilic "the Israelite" (toi Israeleitei) rather than "Ezrahite."
notes.87:8: "Surging waves" renders Greek meteorismous (lit. "upliftings" or "swells"), and "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, denoting a musical pause throughout the Septuagint Psalter.
notes.87:11: The Septuagint translates the Hebrew term for departed shades (rephaim) as iatroi ("physicians"), asking whether human healers can raise the dead to give praise.
notes.87:15: The Greek text reads ten proseuchen mou ("my prayer") rather than "my soul," and in verse 19 apo talaiporias ("because of misery") rather than "darkness."
notes.88:3: The Septuagint reads second-person eipas ("You said") rather than first-person "I said," while retaining second-person "Your truth" in the following clause.
notes.88:11: Greek hyperephanon ("the proud one") renders the Hebrew name Rahab descriptively rather than as a proper name.
notes.88:13: The Greek reads thalassas ("the seas") rather than "the south," and uses the plural transliterated name Hermonim (Hermonieim) for Mount Hermon.
notes.88:21: The Greek text reads en eleei hagioi ("with holy mercy") rather than the similar-sounding elaioi ("oil"), a well-attested Septuagint reading preserved faithfully here.
notes.88:51: The Greek text reads second-person hypeschou ("You sustained") rather than the first-person variant hypeschon ("I bore").
notes.89:2: The Greek text ends with "You are" without the word "God" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text, as the Septuagint appears to have read the corresponding Hebrew consonants as the opening negative of verse 3.
notes.89:5: The Greek reads "Their worthless things shall be years," differing markedly from the Masoretic Text ("You sweep them away; they are like a sleep").
notes.89:9: Literally "our years practiced/meditated as a spider's web," portraying human life as frail, fleeting toil, whereas the Masoretic Text compares our years to a sigh.
notes.89:10: The Greek text reads "in years" (en eniautois) and concludes with "for gentleness has come upon us, and we shall be disciplined," contrasting with the Masoretic Text ("for it is soon gone, and we fly away").
notes.89:12: The Greek reads "Make known Your right hand," while the infinitive "to reckon it up" closes verse 11, differing from the Masoretic division and reading ("So teach us to number our days").
notes.90:1: The Septuagint adds the superscription attributing the psalm to David and reads "in the help of the Most High" and "of the God of heaven," where the Masoretic Text reads "in the secret place" and "of the Almighty."
notes.90:3: "A troubling word" reflects the Septuagint reading the Hebrew consonants for "pestilence" as "word"; the same consonantal vocalization underlies "a thing" in verse 6.
notes.90:6: "A noonday demon" is the distinctive Septuagint rendering corresponding to "the destruction that wastes at noonday" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.90:13: The Greek reads "asp and basilisk" in the first clause, where the Masoretic Text reads "lion and cobra."
notes.91:6: This Greek text reads "weighty" (ebarynthesan) rather than the variant "deep" (ebathynthesan) found in other Greek manuscripts and the Masoretic Text.
notes.91:8: The verb "peered forth" (diekysan) literally denotes peeping or looking out, reflecting a different sense of the Hebrew root translated "blossom" or "flourish" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.91:11: "Unicorn" translates Greek monokerotos ("one-horned beast"), the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew wild ox; "my old age" also reflects a distinct Septuagint reading where the Masoretic Text has "I have been anointed."
notes.91:15: This Greek text begins with "then" (tote) rather than the variant "still" (eti), and verse 16 reads "the Lord my God" where the Masoretic Text reads "my rock."
notes.92:1: The Septuagint superscription assigns this psalm to the day before the Sabbath (Friday), linking it to the sixth day of creation when the earth was settled; this title is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.92:4: The opening phrase renders Greek apo phonon reflecting a Hebrew comparative construction (also readable causally as "from the voices of many waters"), and meteorismoi denotes the surging swells of the sea.
notes.93:1: The Septuagint superscription assigns this psalm to the fourth day of the week (Wednesday), and eparresiasato ("has revealed Himself boldly") conveys open, unrestrained divine manifestation.
notes.93:15: In the Greek text, "righteousness" is the subject that returns to "judgment" (reversing the order in the Hebrew Masoretic Text), and "Interlude" translates diapsalma, the Septuagint liturgical direction corresponding to Hebrew selah.
notes.93:17: The Greek reads to hade ("in Hades," the realm of the dead) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in silence."
notes.93:19: Greek egapesan literally means "loved" or "cherished," expressing affectionate comfort where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "delighted."
notes.94:4: The opening clause, "For the Lord will not reject His people," is a distinctive Septuagint reading absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 95:4 (compare 93:14).
notes.94:6: The Septuagint reads klausomen ("let us weep"), a distinctive Greek reading where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "let us kneel."
notes.94:8: Greek parapikrasmos ("provocation") and peirasmos ("testing") translate the Hebrew place names Meribah and Massah according to their meanings, as also reflected in Hebrews 3:8.
notes.94:11: "They shall surely not enter into My rest" translates the Semitic oath idiom Ei eiseleusontai (literally "If they shall enter"), expressing an emphatic solemn negation.
notes.95:1: The Septuagint superscription ("When the house is being built after the captivity; a song of David") is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 96), linking the psalm to the post-exilic rebuilding of the temple.
notes.95:5: The Greek renders the gods of the nations as daimonia ("demons"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "idols" or "worthless things."
notes.95:6: The Septuagint reads exomologesis ("thanksgiving" or "confession") and "beauty," followed by "holiness and magnificence," differing from the Hebrew terms for splendor, majesty, and strength.
notes.95:9: The Greek reads "in His holy court" (en aule hagia autou), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the splendor of holiness."
notes.95:10: The Septuagint uses the active verb katortosen ("He has firmly established") rather than the passive "is established," and the aorist ebasileusen ("reigns") functions as an ingressive aorist proclaiming the Lord's royal enthronement.
notes.96:1: The Septuagint superscription ("Of David, when his land is being established") has no counterpart in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 97); "his land" refers to David's realm.
notes.96:7: The Greek reads "all His angels" (pantes hoi angeloi autou), the wording cited in Hebrews 1:6, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "all gods."
notes.96:8: The Septuagint uses the Greek regional name "Judea" (Ioudaias) corresponding to "Judah" in the Hebrew text.
notes.96:11: The Greek verb aneteilen ("has dawned" or "has risen") reflects a different Hebrew vocalization or reading than the Masoretic Text's "is sown."
notes.97:1: The Septuagint superscription adds "of David" to the Hebrew heading "A Psalm" (Psalm 98).
notes.97:2: The Greek critical text groups "before the nations" with the first clause ("has made known His salvation before the nations") rather than with the second clause as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.97:3: The Septuagint includes "toward Jacob" in parallel with "toward the house of Israel," an addition not found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.97:6: The Greek specifies elatais ("hammered" or beaten-metal) trumpets and ends with the dative Kyrio ("to the Lord") alongside "before the King," unifying the acclamation directed to the Lord as King.
notes.98:1: The Greek superscription "A Psalm of David" is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew (Psalm 99). The verb rendered "be enraged" (orgizesthosan) reflects the Septuagint reading, whereas the Hebrew is commonly translated "tremble."
notes.98:4: The Greek reads "honor" (time) of a king rather than the Masoretic "strength," and "uprightness" renders the plural Greek noun euthytetas.
notes.98:6: In this Greek text, "He is holy" (hagios estin) stands at the beginning of verse 6 without "for," concluding the liturgical refrain of verse 5 (compare verses 3 and 9); other Greek witnesses attach "for He is holy" to the end of verse 5.
notes.98:8: The Greek reads "all their practices" (panta ta epitedeumata auton), including "all," which is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.99:2: The Greek agalliasis means "exultation" or "exceeding joy," where the Masoretic Hebrew (Psalm 100:2) has a term often rendered "singing."
notes.99:3: The Greek "and not we ourselves" (kai ouch hemeis) corresponds to the written Hebrew (ketib) rather than the marginal reading (qere) "and we are His."
notes.99:4: The Greek reads "with hymns" (en hymnois) and "praise" (aineite) His name, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew has "with praise" and "bless" His name.
notes.100:2: The Greek text here reads "in a blameless song" (en ode amomo, as in Codex Vaticanus), whereas verse 6 and other Greek witnesses read "in a blameless way" (en hodo amomo). Beginning with "I walked," the Septuagint renders the royal declarations of verses 2–8 in past (imperfect and aorist) tenses rather than the future tenses typical of Masoretic translations.
notes.100:4: In the Greek versification, "a crooked heart did not cling to me" concludes verse 3, while verse 4 opens with a genitive absolute ("When the wicked one turned aside from me") in which tou ponerou may be taken as either masculine ("the wicked one") or neuter ("evil").
notes.100:5: The Greek "I did not eat" (ou synesthion) reflects a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonantal root from the Masoretic reading usually translated "I will not endure."
notes.100:7: The Greek reads "practiced arrogance" (poion hyperephanian), where the Masoretic Hebrew (Psalm 101:7) reads "practices deceit."
notes.101:9: The Greek reads "those who praised me" (hoi epainountes me), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "those who deride/rage against me."
notes.101:24: The Greek reads "He answered Him in the way of his strength," reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew verb ("answered" rather than "afflicted/weakened") and introducing the closing appeal to God as direct speech.
notes.101:27: The Greek reads "You shall roll them up" (helixeis), a reading also reflected in the New Testament quotation of this passage at Hebrews 1:12.
notes.102:2: The Greek text here reads "all His praises" (pasas tas aineseis autou), whereas other Septuagint manuscripts and the Hebrew Masoretic Text read "all His benefits/recompenses."
notes.102:14: The Greek shifts to an imperative addressed directly to God, "remember that we are dust" (mnestheti), in contrast to the third-person indicative ("He remembers") in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.102:16: The Greek makes the man the subject and "his place" (ton topon autou) the direct object ("he shall no longer recognize his place"), reversing the subject and object of the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("its place knows it no more").
notes.103:1: The Greek text includes the superscription "Of David," doubles the address "Lord, Lord," and renders the royal attributes as "praise" (exomologesis) and "splendor" (euprepeia).
notes.103:6: The Greek masculine pronoun "His" (autou) grammatically refers back to God—echoing the garment imagery of verse 2—rather than to the feminine noun "earth."
notes.103:16: The Greek reads "the trees of the plain" (tou pediou), reflecting a Septuagint textual tradition distinct from the Masoretic Hebrew "trees of the LORD."
notes.103:17: This Greek critical text reads the singular dative "for it" (auto) with "leads the way" (hegeitai), whereas some other Greek witnesses read the plural genitive "takes the lead over them" (auton).
notes.103:26: This Greek critical text omits the clause concerning ships passing through, moving directly from the sea creatures of verse 25 to the "dragon" (drakon) fashioned to play in the sea.
notes.104:18: The Greek literally reads "his soul passed through iron," with "his soul" as the grammatical subject and "iron" as the object, differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.104:22: The Greek reads "to instruct his princes as himself," reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew from the Masoretic Text ("to bind his princes at his pleasure").
notes.104:28: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("they did not rebel against His word"), the Greek has no negation and reads "they embittered His words."
notes.104:30: The Greek text here reads "kingdoms" (basileion) rather than "kings" (basileon).
notes.104:36: The Greek "labor" (ponou) reflects a different understanding of the underlying Hebrew term rendered "strength" in the Masoretic Text.
notes.105:7: The Greek reads 'as they went up' (anabainontes), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's 'by the sea.'
notes.105:15: The Greek has 'fullness' (plesmonen, meaning satiety), contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'leanness' or 'wasting disease.'
notes.105:28: The Greek verb etelesthesan specifically denotes ritual initiation into the cultic rites of Baal-Peor.
notes.105:32: The Greek translates Hebrew Meribah as 'Contradiction' (Antilogias), highlighting the people's contentious opposition.
notes.105:48: The Greek concludes the doxology with a single 'So be it' (Genoito, translating Hebrew Amen), without the concluding 'Hallelujah' found in the Masoretic Text.
notes.106:3: The Greek literally reads "the sea" (thalasses), preserving the Septuagint directional term where the Masoretic Text is often rendered "the south."
notes.106:17: The Greek reads "He helped them" (antelabeto auton), reflecting a different reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text's "fools."
notes.106:30: The Greek text here reads epimelia ("by the care") rather than the variant epi limena ("to a harbor") attested in some Septuagint witnesses.
notes.106:35: The Greek reads limenas ("havens," a variant of limnas, "pools") and omits the second clause ("and a dry land into watersprings") found in other witnesses and the Masoretic Text.
notes.107:3: The Greek reads "I will awake at dawn" (exegerthesomai orthrou), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "I will awaken the dawn."
notes.107:8: The Greek renders Hebrew Succoth as "the valley of tabernacles" (ton skenomaton) and reads "I will be exalted" (Hypsothesomai) rather than "I will exult."
notes.107:10: The Greek reads "the basin of My hope" (tes elpidos mou) where the Masoretic Text has "My washbasin," uses Idumea (Idoumaia) for Edom, and renders the Philistines as "the foreigners" (hoi allophyloi).
notes.108:1: "To the end" renders the Septuagint superscription Eis to telos, corresponding to the Hebrew musical heading often translated "To the Chief Musician."
notes.108:4: The Greek infinitive phrase anti tou agapan me is syntactically ambiguous, meaning either "instead of loving me" (with "me" as object) or "in return for my loving them" (with "me" as subject, paralleling v. 5).
notes.108:6: Greek diabolos means "accuser" or "slanderer," fitting the judicial imagery of v. 7, though later tradition also associated the term with the devil.
notes.108:23: The Greek text reads the third-person passive verb antanerethe ("is taken away") with "shadow" as its subject, followed by the first-person "I was shaken off," and plural "locusts."
notes.108:24: "Because of oil" renders the literal Septuagint prepositional phrase di' elaion, which reflects a Hebrew idiom expressing the lack of oil or fatness.
notes.109:1: In this messianic psalm (Psalm 110 in the Hebrew numbering), the Septuagint uses kyrios for both "the Lord" (God) and "my Lord" (the Davidic king).
notes.109:3: The Septuagint reads "With You is dominion... in the splendor of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten You," a distinctive reading differing from the vocalized Hebrew text and widely cited in early Christian theology.
notes.109:6: "He shall heap up corpses" translates the concise Greek expression plerosei ptoma (literally "He shall fill [with] fallen bodies" or "complete the downfall"), and the Septuagint reads plural "heads" rather than singular "head."
notes.110:2: "Sought out according to all His desires" follows the Septuagint exezetemena eis panta ta thelemata autou, whereas the Hebrew text reads "studied by all who delight in them."
notes.110:3: The Septuagint translates the opening noun as exomologesis ("thanksgiving" or "confession"), reflecting a different root understanding from the Hebrew "splendor."
notes.110:10: The Greek feminine singular pronoun auten ("it") refers back to "wisdom" (or "understanding") rather than plural "them" (His commandments) as in the Hebrew text.
notes.111:3: The Greek reads "glory and wealth" (doxa kai ploutos), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "wealth and riches."
notes.111:4: The three adjectives "merciful, and compassionate, and righteous" appear without an explicit subject in the Greek; they may describe the righteous man of the psalm or, as often understood liturgically, the Lord Himself.
notes.111:5: Greek logous ("words") reflects a Hebrew term that also denotes "affairs" or "matters," pointing to ordering one's speech or dealings with justice.
notes.112:1: Greek paides can mean either "servants" or "children"; unlike the Hebrew text ("servants of the Lord ... the name of the Lord"), the Greek reads simply "servants" and "His name."
notes.112:3: The Greek verb aineitai is present passive indicative ("is praised"), expressing ongoing universal praise rather than the gerundive sense ("is to be praised") in the Hebrew text and some Greek witnesses.
notes.112:9: The Greek participle euphrainomenon is genitive plural modifying "children" ("rejoicing children"), whereas the Hebrew text and other Greek manuscripts make the mother the joyful one.
notes.113:2: The Greek reads Ioudaia ("Judea") where the Hebrew text reads "Judah."
notes.113:6: This Greek text preserves a shorter reading, omitting the parallel clause about the hills found in the Hebrew text and other Greek manuscripts.
notes.113:7: The Greek verb esaleuthe is aorist passive indicative ("was shaken"), narrating a past event rather than issuing the imperative ("Tremble!") of the Hebrew text.
notes.113:9: In Septuagint numbering, Psalm 113 unites what the Hebrew Masoretic Text divides into Psalm 114 (vv. 1-8) and Psalm 115 (vv. 9-26).
notes.113:25: Unlike the Hebrew text, which speaks of the Lord in the third person and of descending into "silence," the Greek addresses the Lord directly ("You, O Lord") and names the realm of the dead as "Hades."
notes.114:1: This Greek text reads "God" (ho theos) rather than "the Lord" as in other Septuagint witnesses, omits an explicit object after "I have loved," and uses the future tense "will hear."
notes.114:2: The Greek text reads "in His days" (en tais hemerais autou), differing from manuscripts and the Hebrew tradition that read "in my days."
notes.114:6: Greek ta nepia literally means "the infants" or "the little ones," rendering the Hebrew term for "the simple."
notes.114:9: Greek euaresteso ("I will be well-pleasing") renders the Hebrew idiom of walking before the Lord, echoing Septuagint usage in passages such as Genesis 5:22 and 5:24.
notes.115:2: Greek ekstasis denotes sudden alarm, bewilderment, or dismay, here translated "dismay."
notes.115:3: This Greek text reads peri hon ("for what") without the word "all" found in some Septuagint manuscripts.
notes.115:6: Verse 115:5 (which repeats the vow clause of 115:9 in some witnesses) is absent from this Greek text, following major Septuagint manuscripts.
notes.115:8: This Greek text concludes after "a sacrifice of praise," omitting the additional clause ("and I will call upon the name of the Lord") present in other witnesses.
notes.116:1: This Greek text uses the third-person imperative ainesatosan ("let all the peoples praise Him," matching Romans 15:11) rather than the second-person imperative found in some manuscripts.
notes.117:1: The Septuagint opens this psalm with "Hallelujah" (absent in the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 118) and includes the clause "that He is good" in verses 2 through 4.
notes.117:12: The Greek uniquely adds "around a honeycomb" and reads "they blazed up" (contrasting with the Hebrew "were extinguished"); throughout verses 10 through 12, the Greek verb means to repel or ward off.
notes.117:16: The Greek critical text preserves the shorter form of this verse, reading "exalted me" transitively and omitting the repeated clause "the right hand of the Lord has acted mightily."
notes.117:27: The Septuagint reads "appeared to us" (ἐπέφανεν) and "appoint a feast with thick boughs," differing from the Masoretic Text's "given us light" and "bind the festival sacrifice with cords."
notes.117:28: The Greek text includes a third clause repeating the thanksgiving formula of verse 21, which is not present in the Masoretic Text.
notes.118:1: The Septuagint opens Psalm 118 (corresponding to Psalm 119 in Hebrew numbering) with the heading "Hallelujah" (Greek Halleluia), which is absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.118:25: The Greek text reads the future indicative zesomai ("I shall live"), whereas the Masoretic Text and some Septuagint witnesses read an imperative ("give me life").
notes.118:26: The Greek text reads tas hodous sou ("Your ways"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "my ways."
notes.118:38: The Greek text preserves the preposition eis before to logion sou (literally "establish for Your servant in Your oracle"), an early Septuagint reading that differs from manuscripts taking "Your oracle" as the direct object.
notes.118:41: The Greek text repeats kata to eleos sou ("according to Your mercy") at the end of the verse, whereas the Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses read "according to Your word."
notes.118:47: Both verses 47 and 48 read the second-person verb egapesas ("which You have loved exceedingly"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read the first person ("which I have loved").
notes.118:50: The Greek text reads hoti to logion sou ouk exeklina ("for I have not turned aside from Your oracle"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read "for Your word has given me life."
notes.118:75: The Greek text makes "Your judgments" the subject of the plural verb etapeinosan ("have humbled me") with two adverbial datives ("in righteousness and truth"), differing from witnesses that read "Your judgments are righteousness, and in truth You have humbled me."
notes.118:82: The Greek text reads the third-person plural indicative Parekalesan me ("They have comforted me"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read a question, "When will You comfort me?"
notes.118:85: The Septuagint reads "recounted idle tales" (adoleschias) rather than the Masoretic Text's "dug pits," and adds the vocative "O Lord" at the end of the verse.
notes.118:95: The Greek text contains only the second clause ("Yet Your testimonies I have understood"), omitting the opening clause ("Sinners waited for me to destroy me") found in the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses.
notes.118:102: The Greek text reads klimaton ("regions" or "inclinations"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read krimaton ("judgments").
notes.118:114: The Greek text reads ton laon sou ("Your people"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read ton logon sou ("Your word").
notes.118:120: The Septuagint renders the Hebrew verb for shuddering in fear as katheloson ("nail down" or "pierce with nails").
notes.118:124: The Greek text reads kata to logion sou ("according to Your oracle") and adds kata ("according to") before "Your ordinances," whereas the Masoretic Text and other Greek witnesses read "according to Your mercy" and "teach me Your statutes."
notes.118:139: The Greek text reads "zeal for Your house" (ho zelos tou oikou sou) and "Your commandments," differing from the Masoretic Text ("my zeal" and "Your words").
notes.118:147: The Greek text reads the third-person plural proephthasan me ("they came upon me" or "they overtook me"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read the first-person singular ("I rose before dawn").
notes.118:148: The Greek text reads pros se orthroun ("rising early toward You"), differing from witnesses that read pros orthron ("before dawn").
notes.118:149: The Greek text reads kata to logion sou ("according to Your oracle"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read "according to Your mercy."
notes.118:176: The Greek text reads zeson ton doulon sou ("give life to Your servant"), whereas the Masoretic Text and other Septuagint witnesses read zeteson ("seek Your servant").
notes.119:3: The Greek uses the prepositional phrase pros glossan dolian ("against a deceitful tongue") rather than addressing the tongue directly in the vocative as in the Hebrew text.
notes.119:4: The Septuagint translates the desert-shrub coals with the adjective eremikois ("of the wilderness" or "desert"), emphasizing desolation.
notes.119:5: Where the Hebrew Masoretic Text names the region of Meshech, the Greek reads a verb meaning "prolonged" (he paroikia mou emakrynthe, "my sojourning has been prolonged").
notes.119:7: The Greek adds dorean ("without cause"), heightening the unprovoked hostility of the speaker's adversaries; in this Greek text, "with those who hate peace" is joined to verse 6.
notes.120:3: The Greek opens with a second-person prohibition (me dos, "Do not give") addressed to the hearer, rather than a third-person statement about God as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.120:4: This Greek text reads exypnosei (an intensive compound of hypnoo, "fall fast asleep"), where other Septuagint manuscripts read the simple verb hypnosei ("sleep").
notes.120:7: The verb shifts from the future indicative phylaxei ("shall guard") in the first clause to the aorist optative phylaxai ("may He guard") in the second, turning assurance into a benediction.
notes.120:8: The Septuagint reads ten eisodon sou kai ten exodon sou ("your coming in and your going out"), reversing the Hebrew order ("going out and coming in").
notes.121:2: The Greek reads "in the courts of Jerusalem" (en tais aulais Ierousalem) without a possessive pronoun, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "within your gates, O Jerusalem."
notes.121:3: The Greek metoche ("sharing, participation, fellowship") with epi to auto ("together, as one") portrays Jerusalem's unity in terms of communal fellowship rather than architectural compactness.
notes.121:6: This Greek text reverses the usual clause order of verse 6, placing "and prosperity for those who love you" before the command to seek Jerusalem's peace, and uses the dative "for Jerusalem" (te Ierousalem).
notes.121:7: The Greek includes the possessive pronoun in "your peace" (eirene sou), renders the Hebrew word for "rampart" as dynamei ("strength"), and uses the rare compound pyrgobaresin ("fortified towers").
notes.121:9: This Greek text reads exezetesa soi without agatha ("good things," found in other witnesses), leaving the object of "sought out" implied from "peace" in verse 8.
notes.122:1: The superscription literally means "A Song of the Steps" (or Ascents). The Greek reads singular "in heaven" rather than plural "in the heavens."
notes.122:2: The Greek uses plural "hands" in both comparisons and employs a verb for "compassion" distinct from "have mercy" in verse 3.
notes.122:4: The Greek uses nominative nouns with datives ("reproach to those who prosper, and contempt to the proud"), which can be read either as a verdict against them or as a literal rendering of the Hebrew preposition describing their scorn.
notes.123:1: The Greek superscription does not include "of David," and the text reads "among us" (en hemin) rather than "on our side."
notes.123:4: The Greek reads singular "the water" and makes "our soul" the grammatical subject passing through the torrent (and likewise in verse 5), whereas the Hebrew has the torrent passing over the soul.
notes.123:5: Greek anupostaton literally denotes that which cannot be withstood or endured, hence "irresistible" or "overwhelming."
notes.123:7: The Greek specifically reads "a sparrow" (strouthion) and "the hunters" (ton thereuonton), and uses the passive verb "was delivered / were delivered" rather than "escaped."
notes.124:1: Unlike the Hebrew verse division, the Greek places "Jerusalem" at the end of verse 1 as the object of "he who dwells in," making the inhabitant of Jerusalem the subject of "shall never be shaken."
notes.124:3: The Greek makes the Lord the active subject ("He will not leave") and reads "of sinners" rather than the abstract "of wickedness."
notes.125:1: Greek parakeklemenoi ("who have been comforted") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("who dream"), reflecting a different reading of the Hebrew consonants.
notes.125:2: Greek charas ("joy") corresponds to "laughter" in the Hebrew text, and the future verb erousin ("they shall say") casts the nations' confession forward in time.
notes.125:4: Greek uses the singular ho cheimarrous ("the torrent," a winter-flowing stream) and renders the Hebrew Negev as to noto ("the south").
notes.125:6: Greek employs plural verbs and participles throughout rather than the Hebrew singular, and pairs participles with finite verbs to mirror the emphatic Hebrew idiom.
notes.126:2: Greek egeiresthai meta to kathesthai ("to rise up after sitting down") and hotan do tois agapetois autou ("when He gives... to His beloved ones") differ in sense and number from the Hebrew text.
notes.126:3: Greek reads the genitive tou karpou tes gastros autes ("of the fruit of her womb"), linking "the reward" directly to the offspring in apposition.
notes.126:4: Greek ton ektetinagmenon ("of those who have been shaken out") derives the underlying Hebrew word from the root meaning "to shake out" rather than "youth."
notes.126:5: Greek ten epithymian autou ("his desire") stands in place of the Hebrew "his quiver," and the Greek shifts from singular ("he shall not be put to shame") to plural ("when they speak to their enemies").
notes.127:2: Greek tous karpous ton ponon sou ("the fruits of your labors") corresponds to "the labor of your hands" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.127:3: Greek en tois klitesi ("along the sides," indicating the inner sides or walls of a house) and neophyta ("newly planted shoots") render the domestic imagery literally.
notes.127:5: Greek uses optative verbs ("May the Lord bless... may you see," continuing into verse 6) for a formal priestly blessing and renders Jerusalem's prosperity with the plural ta agatha ("the good things").
notes.128:3: The Greek reads "the sinners hammered" (or "worked as craftsmen") and "prolonged their iniquity," differing from the Hebrew tradition's "the plowers plowed" and "made long their furrows."
notes.128:4: The Greek reads "the neck of sinners," whereas the Hebrew tradition reads "the cords of the wicked."
notes.128:8: This Greek text reads "upon us" and the future "we will bless you," rather than "upon you" and "we bless you."
notes.129:4: The Greek term hilasmos denotes propitiation or forgiveness. The Greek lacks the Hebrew clause "that You may be feared," instead opening the next sentence with "For the sake of Your name" at the end of verse 4.
notes.129:5: The Greek reads "for His law" rather than "in His word," shifting briefly from direct address ("O Lord") to third-person reference ("His law").
notes.129:6: Following the Greek critical text, this verse reads "from the morning watch until night," without the Hebrew comparison to watchmen waiting for the morning or the repeated line found in some manuscripts.
notes.130:1: This Greek text omits the attribution "of David" found in the superscription of the Hebrew tradition and some manuscripts.
notes.130:2: This Greek text differs notably from both the Hebrew and some Septuagint manuscripts, punctuating after "humble-minded" (literally "if I was not humble-minded," functioning idiomatically as an adversative affirmation after the preceding negatives) and reading "and I lifted up my soul" and "until You recompense my soul."
notes.131:1: The Greek reads "meekness" (πρᾳύτητος), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "affliction" or "hardship."
notes.131:4: The Greek text includes the third clause "nor rest to my temples," which is not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.131:6: The Greek text reads "in the thickets of the forest" (ἐν ταῖς δασέσι τοῦ δρυμοῦ), differing from other Septuagint witnesses ("plains of the forest") and the Hebrew ("fields of the woods/Jaar").
notes.131:7: The Greek text shifts from first-person singular ("I will enter," εἰσελεύσομαι) to first-person plural ("we will worship") and reads "at the place where His feet stood" where the Hebrew has "at His footstool."
notes.131:15: The Greek text reads "her widow" (τὴν χήραν αὐτῆς), a well-attested Septuagint reading alongside "her hunt/catch" (θήραν) in other Greek manuscripts and "her provision" in the Hebrew.
notes.131:17: The Greek text reads "for your anointed" (τῷ χριστῷ σου), shifting to second-person address within the divine promise, whereas other Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew read "for My anointed."
notes.132:1: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Greek heading omits "of David" and frames the verse as a rhetorical question ("what is good or what is pleasant, except...").
notes.133:1: The Greek text reads "who stand in the courts of the house of our God" without the additional clause "in the house of the Lord," and places "in the nights" at the opening of verse 2.
notes.134:1: The Greek opens with the transliterated "Hallelujah" and places "Lord" in the accusative as the direct object of "praise," addressing "servants" without the genitive "of the Lord" found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.134:12: The Greek reads "Israel His servant," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Israel His people."
notes.134:14: This Greek text reads "has compassion on" (oikteirei) rather than "will judge" (krinei / MT yadin), paired with "will be comforted" (paraklethesetai), expressing God's consoling mercy toward His servants.
notes.134:18: The Greek uses the optative mood (genointo), expressing an imprecatory wish ("May ... become") rather than a simple declarative statement.
notes.135:6: The Greek uses the singular "water" with the verb stereosanti ("made firm"), echoing the creation vocabulary of Genesis 1.
notes.135:7: The Greek adds "alone" (mono), paralleling verse 4 and not present here in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.135:10: The Greek reads "Egypt together with their firstborn" rather than "Egypt in their firstborn."
notes.135:26: This Greek text reads "the Lord of heaven" (to kyrio tou ouranou) rather than "the God of heaven" found in the Masoretic Text and some Septuagint witnesses.
notes.136:1: The Greek includes the superscription "Of David," which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.136:2: The Greek organa refers to musical instruments generally rather than specifically harps or lyres as in the Hebrew text.
notes.136:5: The Greek uses the passive optative ("may my right hand be forgotten"), differing from the active sense in the Hebrew text ("let my right hand forget [its skill]").
notes.136:8: The Greek calls Babylon "wretched" (he talaiporos), rendering the underlying Hebrew as "miserable" or "devastated" rather than "doomed to destruction."
notes.137:1: The Greek includes "for You have heard the words of my mouth" and reads "before the angels" (angelon), whereas the Masoretic Text omits the former clause and reads "before the gods."
notes.137:2: The Greek reads "You have magnified Your holy name above all things" (also syntactically possible as "Your holy sanctuary above every name"), differing from the Masoretic Text ("Your word above all Your name").
notes.137:7: This Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus) reads "against the wrath of enemies You stretched out my hands," whereas other Greek witnesses and the Masoretic Text read "of my enemies You stretched out Your hand."
notes.138:9: This Greek text reads kat' orthon ("straight ahead"), whereas other Greek manuscripts read kat' orthron ("at dawn").
notes.138:12: This Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus) preserves the shorter reading, omitting the clauses "for darkness shall not be darkened from You, and night shall be illuminated as day" found in other Greek manuscripts and the Masoretic Text.
notes.138:16: This Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus) reads "My eyes saw Your unwrought work," reversing the pronouns found in other Greek manuscripts and the Masoretic Text ("Your eyes saw my unformed substance").
notes.138:20: The Greek reflects a notably different reading of the underlying Hebrew consonants, yielding "You will say concerning reasoning, 'They shall take Your cities in vain.'"
notes.138:24: This Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus) reads ei ides anomias ("if You have seen iniquities"), whereas other Greek manuscripts read ei hodos anomias ("if there is a way of iniquity").
notes.139:4: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma (also in verses 6 and 9), the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew selah, denoting a musical or liturgical pause.
notes.139:9: The Greek reads "from my desire" (apo tes epithymias mou), taking the noun as first-person singular rather than "the desires of the wicked" as in the Masoretic Text.
notes.139:12: In this Greek text (as in Codex Vaticanus), "on the earth" stands in verse 11 and verse 12 omits the opening clause "a talkative man shall not be established" found in other Greek witnesses and the Masoretic Text.
notes.140:4: The verb translated "join with" reflects Greek syndoiaso (a spelling of syndyazo, "associate or consort with"), and "their chosen ones" renders ton eklekton auton, which can also denote "their choice delicacies."
notes.140:5: Literally "for yet again and again my prayer is in their good pleasures," preserving the Septuagint reading eudokiais ("good pleasures") rather than harmonizing to "evil deeds."
notes.140:6: The Greek text reads edynethesan ("they have prevailed" or "were able"), a textual variant alongside hedynthesan ("they were sweetened" or "pleasant").
notes.140:10: The singular pronoun in "his net" (autou) follows the Greek wording literally and may refer either to the sinner's own snare or to a net of divine judgment.
notes.141:1: "Of understanding" translates Greek syneseos, the Septuagint equivalent of the Hebrew superscription term Maskil.
notes.141:5: The Greek uses first-person past verbs ("I looked... and watched") rather than second-person imperatives.
notes.141:8: The Greek reads "wait for me" (hypomenousin), differing from textual traditions that read "surround me."
notes.142:1: The superscription includes the Septuagint historical notice "when his son pursued him," linking the psalm to Absalom's rebellion.
notes.142:3: This Greek text begins directly with "He has brought my life low," without the opening clause ("For the enemy has pursued my soul") present in other witnesses.
notes.142:6: "Interlude" translates Greek diapsalma, a liturgical or musical pause corresponding to Hebrew Selah.
notes.142:10: This Greek text reads "Your Holy Spirit" (to hagion) rather than "Your good Spirit," and "in the straight way" renders en te eutheia without an explicit noun for "land."
notes.143:1: The superscription "against Goliath" is unique to the Septuagint; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads only "Of David."
notes.143:3: The Greek passive verb literally reads "that You were made known to him," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "that You know him."
notes.143:10: In the Greek text, "From an evil sword" begins the petition completed by "deliver me" in verse 11, rather than modifying "redeems David His servant" as in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.143:12: The Septuagint reads "whose sons" and continues with third-person plural pronouns through verse 14, connecting to verse 15 ("They called blessed"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text shifts to first-person plural ("that our sons").
notes.144:9: The Greek critical text reads "to those who wait patiently" (or "endure"), whereas some Septuagint witnesses and the Hebrew Masoretic Text read "to all."
notes.144:13: The second sentence ("Faithful is the Lord in His words, and holy in all His works") supplies the missing nun-line of the Hebrew alphabetical acrostic, preserved in the Septuagint and Dead Sea Scrolls but absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.144:16: The Greek reads plural "Your hands" and "with goodwill" (or "good pleasure"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "Your hand" and "the desire of every living thing."
notes.145:1: The attribution to the post-exilic prophets Haggai and Zechariah is distinctive to the Septuagint tradition and does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.145:8: The Septuagint places "lifts up those who are cast down" first and reads "makes the blind wise," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text places "opens the eyes of the blind" first.
notes.145:9: The Greek word rendered "sojourners" (proselytous) denotes resident aliens or proselytes living among Israel.
notes.146:1: The Septuagint divides Hebrew Psalm 147 into two psalms (Psalms 146 and 147 here) and prefixes each with the superscription attributing it to the post-exilic prophets Haggai and Zechariah.
notes.146:8: The final clause "and green herbage for the service of men" is distinctive to the Septuagint text (echoing Psalm 103:14 LXX) and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.146:11: The Greek explicitly includes "all" ("with all those who hope in His mercy"), a reading characteristic of the Septuagint.
notes.147:1: In the Septuagint numbering, this begins a distinct psalm (corresponding to Hebrew Psalm 147:12–20) with its own superscription of Haggai and Zechariah.
notes.147:3: "Fat of wheat" renders the literal Greek idiom (stear pyrou) denoting the richest and finest grain.
notes.147:5: The Greek shifts here into genitive participles continuing from "His" in verse 4, and reads "mist" (homichle) where the Hebrew has "frost."
notes.147:9: Unlike the Hebrew text ("they have not known them"), the Greek makes God the subject ("He has not made known to them") and ends without a closing "Hallelujah."
notes.148:3: The Greek coordinates "the light" alongside "all the stars" ("all the stars and the light"), whereas the Hebrew reads "all stars of light" (shining stars).
notes.148:5: The clause "for He spoke, and they came into being" is a distinctive Septuagint reading (paralleling Psalm 32:9 LXX) not present in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.148:7: Greek drakontes denotes dragons or great sea creatures inhabiting the ocean depths.
notes.148:14: This Greek text omits both the phrase "a hymn for all His holy ones" (found in some Septuagint manuscripts and the Hebrew text) and a closing "Hallelujah."
notes.149:4: The Septuagint reads 'will exalt' (hypsosei), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'will adorn' or 'beautify.'
notes.149:6: The Greek literally reads 'the exaltations of God' (echoing 'exalt' in verse four), 'in their throat' (singular), and 'two-edged swords' (plural).
notes.149:8: The Greek distinguishes between fetters for the feet (pedais) and iron manacles for the hands (cheiropedais siderais).
notes.150:1: The Greek plural en tois hagiois autou can mean either 'in His holy places' (His sanctuary) or 'among His saints' (His holy ones).
notes.150:5: Greek euechois means 'well-sounding' or 'melodious,' while alalagmou denotes a loud shout of triumph or jubilation.
notes.150:6: Literally 'every breath,' a poetic expression encompassing all living creatures; 'Hallelujah' renders the Greek transliteration Allelouia.
notes.151:1: Psalm 151 is a supernumerary psalm in the Septuagint, standing 'outside the number' of the one hundred fifty psalms; Greek idiographos denotes something written in one's own hand.
notes.151:4: Greek angelon can mean either 'messenger' (referring to the prophet Samuel who anointed David) or 'angel.'
notes.151:6: Greek allophylos literally means 'foreigner' or 'one of another tribe,' and serves as the Septuagint's standard designation for a Philistine.
notes.151:7: Literally 'having drawn the sword from him,' referring to Goliath's own sword at his side.

unplaced.text: lest my enemy ever say, "I have prevailed against him"; those who afflict me will exult if I am shaken.
unplaced.note: Matches the opening clauses of 12:5 in the site numbering (reading optative eipoi in this witness).
